The Big Bang to a Living Planet
Everything you know started as a tiny, hot dot

Imagine every star, every river and every chai cup you have ever had. All of it was once squeezed into something smaller than an atom. That is where our story starts. We will cover 13.8 billion years in a few minutes. Do not worry about memorising dates. Just enjoy how strange it all is.
The universe begins

About 13.8 billion years ago , space itself began to expand from an extremely hot, dense state. We call this the Big Bang. For the first few hundred thousand years, the universe was a glowing fog. Then it cooled. Hydrogen and helium gathered into clouds. Gravity pulled the clouds together until they ignited. The first stars were born.
You are made of dead stars

The Big Bang made mostly hydrogen and helium. Heavier things, like the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones, were cooked inside stars. When big stars exploded, they scattered those atoms across space. Our Sun and its planets formed from such a cloud about 4.6 billion years ago . Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
A planet gets a Moon

Early Earth was a ball of fire and rock. Most scientists think a Mars-sized body, often called Theia, smashed into it. The debris became our Moon. This is the giant-impact idea, and it is the best-supported explanation we have. The Moon steadies Earth's tilt. That helps keep our climate calm enough for life.
Life, then a poisonous gift

The first living things were tiny single cells. Evidence for life goes back at least 3.5 billion years. Some of these microbes, cyanobacteria, learned to make food from sunlight and gave off oxygen. Oxygen was poison for most life then. Around 2.4 billion years ago it built up in the air in the Great Oxidation Event. It changed the planet for ever.
Animals, extinctions and us

The Cambrian explosion, about 540 million years ago, filled the seas with complex animals. An asteroid struck near today's Mexico 66 million years ago and wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs. Mammals got their chance. In cosmic terms, humans arrived just now.
Was the Big Bang an explosion in space?

Myth: a bomb went off in an empty room. Fact: there was no room. Space itself expanded everywhere at once. There is no centre you can point to. Another common mix-up: the Big Bang does not explain why it happened. Science can describe what happened very soon after, but the very first moment remains an open question.

Out of Africa: How Humans Spread Everywhere
A small band of people walked out and changed the planet

Our species is only about 300,000 years old. Yet today we live on every continent. How did a creature from Africa end up in the Arctic and on remote islands? The answer is a story of grass, coasts, ice and an astonishing amount of walking.
Who counts as human?

Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco date to about 300,000 years ago and show early Homo sapiens. Others have been found in Ethiopia (Omo Kibish, about 230,000 years ago). We were not alone. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia. Denisovans lived in Asia. Other human cousins lived on islands like Flores in Indonesia.
The great walk

Most scientists think the main wave left Africa about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. Some earlier trips happened too, and the dates are still debated. People probably followed coasts and rivers, not a single big march.
We met our cousins, and had children

DNA from old bones shows that people outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. Some Asians and Pacific Islanders carry Denisovan DNA too. Tibetans carry a Denisovan gene that helps them live at high altitude. So we did not just replace our cousins. We mixed with them.
Why did only we survive?

Nobody knows for sure. Possible reasons: bigger social networks, better tools for trade and sharing, new hunting tools, or just bad luck in small, cold populations. The Neanderthals were clever. They made fire, tools and perhaps jewellery. Historians and archaeologists still argue about the main cause.
Empty continents, big consequences

When people reached Australia and the Americas, many giant animals vanished within thousands of years. Climate change played a part. Many experts think hunting did too. The balance is still debated. This was the first time one species reshaped whole ecosystems.
Out of Africa, or many places at once?

The 'multiregional' idea said humans evolved in several regions at the same time. DNA evidence has mostly settled it: all living people descend mainly from Africans. But the mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans means the story is 'Out of Africa, plus some mixing'. Also, one famous myth: 'Neanderthals were dim brutes'. Evidence says they were skilled and cared for their sick.

The Cognitive Revolution and Cave Art
Why would someone crawl into a dark cave to paint a bull?

About 40,000 years ago, people started leaving marks that said 'we were here, and we thought about things'. Painted animals, carved figures, flutes made of bone. Something in the human mind lit up. Let us visit the oldest art galleries on Earth.
The oldest paintings keep getting older

In Indonesia's Sulawesi island, a painted pig has been dated to at least 45,500 years ago , and hand stencils to about 40,000. Some Sulawesi art has now been dated even older, by dating the thin mineral crust over it. The oldest known art keeps moving back as dating improves. That is why you should treat 'oldest' claims as 'oldest so far'.
The cave that was a time capsule

In 1994, three explorers found Chauvet Cave in southern France. It had been sealed by a rockfall for about 20,000 years. Inside: lions, rhinos, horses and bears painted about 30,000-36,000 years ago. Later, Lascaux (France, about 17,000 years old) was found by teenagers chasing a dog, in 1940. Its bulls are huge and gorgeous.
Animals who are half-human

The Lion-man of the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany is a carved ivory figure with a human body and a lion's head. It is about 40,000 years old. It shows people could imagine things that do not exist. Some scholars link this to early belief or stories.
What was going on in their heads?

Historians call this the Cognitive Revolution , a term popularised by Yuval Noah Harari. The big idea: humans got better at language, planning and imagination. But this idea is debated. Some archaeologists think there was no sudden 'revolution'. Neanderthals may have made art too: engravings and painted shells in Spain are claimed to be Neanderthal, though the dating is contested.
Music, jewellery and trade

Bone flutes made from vulture bone and mammoth ivory from caves in Germany are about 40,000 years old . Shell beads travelled hundreds of kilometres. That tells us about trade and identity. Somebody wore beads to say who they were.
Were cave artists 'primitive'?

Myth: cave people were dim. Fact: their brains were the same size as ours. The artists used shading, perspective and clever use of rock bumps to make animals look alive. Something else: nobody knows why they painted. 'Hunting magic', shamans in trances and storytelling are all guesses. Historians argue and none of the guesses is proven.

The Agricultural Revolution: Best or Worst Idea Ever?
The day people started farming, they may have signed up for a harder life
For about 300,000 years people hunted and gathered. Then, around 11,000 years ago, some began to plant seeds. It sounds like progress. But look closer. Was farming a gift, a trap, or both?
Where it began

Farming began independently in several places. The best-known early centre is the Fertile Crescent (modern Iraq, Syria, Turkey, Israel/Palestine, Iran). There, people grew wheat, barley, peas and lentils from about 11,000 years ago. Other centres: rice in the Yangtze valley (China), millet in northern China, maize in Mexico, potatoes in the Andes, and more.
Plants and animals change too
The same happened to animals. Sheep and goats were domesticated about 10,000 years ago, cattle shortly after. Dogs came much earlier, from wolves, long before farming.
The trap

Skeletons of early farmers are often shorter and show more disease than hunter-gatherers'. Diets had less variety. Living close to animals spread new diseases. The historian Yuval Noah Harari called the shift 'history's biggest fraud'. Jared Diamond called it 'the worst mistake' in human history. Others disagree strongly. Farming fed far more people, and it made cities possible.
Surplus, storage and rulers

Farming produced surplus food that could be stored. Whoever controlled the grain store gained power. Some people could stop farming and become priests, soldiers or craftspeople. Populations grew. Settlements became towns. At Çatalhöyük in Turkey (about 7,500 BCE) thousands of people lived in houses packed together, entered through the roof.
Why then?

The last Ice Age ended about 11,700 years ago. The climate became warmer and more stable. Some scholars say that stability made farming possible. Others point to settled hunter-gatherers who began planting by choice. Nobody decided 'let us invent farming'. It was a slow drift over thousands of years.
Was it a revolution at all?

The word 'revolution' suggests a quick change. In truth, the shift took thousands of years. Some groups mixed hunting and farming for a long time. Others never became farmers. Also: farming is not clearly 'worse'. Life expectancy and health improved in some places and fell in others. The honest answer: it depends where and when.

Göbekli Tepe and the First Monuments
The temple that arrived before the farm

Imagine finding a giant stone circle, older than Stonehenge by about 6,000 years, built by people who had not yet invented pottery or the wheel. In 1994, a German archaeologist, Klaus Schmidt, walked up a bare hill in south-east Turkey and noticed something.
A hill full of pillars

Göbekli Tepe (Turkish for 'Potbelly Hill') is near Şanlıurfa. Its tall T-shaped limestone pillars, some about 5 metres high and weighing many tonnes, stand in circles. They date to about 9500-8000 BCE . Many pillars are carved with foxes, boars, snakes, vultures and scorpions. Some pillars look like stylised people, with arms and hands carved on the sides.
Which came first: the temple or the farm?

Schmidt suggested that a gathering place for ritual might have pushed people to settle and farm, because feeding crowds needed food. 'First the temple, then the city', he said. This flips the usual story. Some scholars agree. Others point out that people also lived and worked nearby, so it may not have been only a temple.
They buried it on purpose
After about 1,500 years, the site was filled in deliberately. Nobody knows why. Excavation has uncovered only a small part of the site so far, so we may still be missing the story.
How did they do it?

These builders had no metal tools and no wheels or beasts of burden. They cut pillars with flint tools from a nearby quarry and moved them by rope and muscle. That needed hundreds of people working together. Who organised them? We do not know. There are no kings or written laws from this time to tell us.
Other early monuments

Later, humans built bigger things. Stonehenge 's big stones went up around 2500 BCE. The Megalithic temples of Malta are about 3600-3200 BCE. In Egypt, the first pyramid, Djoser's, was built around 2670 BCE. Göbekli Tepe is older than all of these, by thousands of years.
Was it built by aliens or a lost civilisation?

Myth: some popular shows claim Göbekli Tepe proves a 'lost advanced civilisation'. Fact: there is no evidence for this. The tools, bones and carvings are consistent with hunter-gatherer communities. The truly amazing thing is that ordinary people did it. Archaeologists dislike the 'lost civilisation' idea, and it can dismiss the skill of ancient people.

Sumer: Writing, Cities and the First Laws
Writing was invented to count beer and barley

The most important invention in history started as boring accounting. Around 3300 BCE, in a city called Uruk, someone pressed a reed into wet clay to record who owed what. Welcome to Sumer, in southern Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
The first cities

Sumer had city-states such as Uruk, Ur, Lagash and Kish . By about 3000 BCE, Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people. Each city had its own god, its own king and a temple tower called a ziggurat . Farmers used canals to irrigate barley fields in a hot, dry land. Controlling water meant organising people. That helped create governments.
From tokens to words
The word cuneiform means 'wedge-shaped'. At first it recorded rations and goods. Later it carried letters, poems, spells and laws. Scribes trained for years in schools called edubba .
The first named author was a woman

Enheduanna (about 2300 BCE) was a priestess and daughter of King Sargon of Akkad. She wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna and signed them. She is the first author we know by name. Sargon himself created the first big empire, the Akkadian empire, joining many city-states under one ruler. He is a legend in his own right: the story says he was found as a baby floating in a basket on a river.
A hero and a flood

The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest stories we still have. Gilgamesh was a king of Uruk, probably a real ruler. In the poem he seeks eternal life after his friend Enkidu dies. The epic includes a great flood, long before the Bible's Noah story was written down. The version we know best was written about 1200-1000 BCE, based on older Sumerian stories.
Laws, written down

The oldest surviving law code is that of Ur-Nammu of Ur (about 2100 BCE). The most famous is Hammurabi's of Babylon (about 1754 BCE), carved on a black stone pillar now in the Louvre in Paris. Hammurabi's laws often punished by 'eye for an eye'. But punishment depended on rank: harming a noble cost more than harming a commoner.
Was Hammurabi's code the first law?

Myth: Hammurabi wrote the world's first laws. Fact: Ur-Nammu's and others came centuries earlier. Hammurabi's is simply the best preserved. Historians also argue about whether it was a law book used in courts or a royal showpiece that praised the king as a just ruler. Both could be true.

Egypt: Pharaohs, Pyramids and the Afterlife
Cleopatra lived closer to us than to the pyramids

Here is a fact to win any chai-time argument. The Great Pyramid was built about 2560 BCE. Cleopatra lived about 2,500 years later. The Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her. Egypt is old in a way that is hard to feel. Let us feel it.
A gift of the Nile

Egypt is a thin green strip in a desert. Each summer the Nile flooded, leaving rich black mud. Farming there was easy and predictable, so Egypt grew rich. Around 3100 BCE , Upper and Lower Egypt were joined under one king. Tradition names him Menes or Narmer. Egyptians called the ruler 'pharaoh' (from per-aa , 'great house') in later times.
Pyramids

The first pyramid, built for Djoser by his architect Imhotep , stacked six huge steps. Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza was once about 146 metres tall. It was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.
Who built them?

Not slaves. At Giza archaeologists found a workers' town with bakeries, breweries and graves. Workers were fed beef, bread and beer, and some were buried near the pyramids with honour. Teams of farmers probably joined the work during the Nile flood, when fields were underwater. It was a national project, a bit like paying taxes in labour.
The afterlife business

Egyptians believed the dead went on a journey. The heart was weighed against a feather of the goddess Ma'at . If it was light, you passed to a happy afterlife. To keep the body, they made mummies. It took about 70 days and removed the organs. The brain was often pulled out through the nose and thrown away. The heart was left in.
Rulers, a boy and a stone

Hatshepsut ruled as king (about 1479-1458 BCE) and was shown with a beard. Tutankhamun was a minor king, yet his nearly untouched tomb, found by Howard Carter in 1922 , held over 5,000 objects. Hieroglyphs were a mystery until the Rosetta Stone (found 1799). Jean-François Champollion cracked them in 1822 by comparing the Egyptian with its Greek text.
Did a pharaoh's curse kill the Tut team?

Myth: opening Tutankhamun's tomb brought a deadly curse. Fact: Lord Carnarvon died in 1923 of an infected mosquito bite that turned into blood poisoning. Carter lived until 1939. Studies show people involved in the opening lived about as long as anyone else. The curse was a newspaper sensation.

Shang and Zhou China: Oracle Bones and the Mandate of Heaven
Fortune-telling is where Chinese writing began

Imagine a king who wants to ask the gods, 'Will it rain? Will my toothache end? Should I attack?' He gives a priest a turtle shell and a hot poker. The cracks answer. And the question is scratched into the shell. That is the oldest Chinese writing we have.
The Shang dynasty

The Shang ruled the Yellow River region from about 1600 to 1046 BCE (dates are approximate). Their late capital was Anyang , where archaeologists dug up palaces, tombs, and horse chariots. They made superb bronze ritual vessels, huge and decorated. Kings were also priests who talked to their ancestors.
How an oracle bone worked
Over 150,000 pieces have been found. Their script, about 1250 BCE and later, is clearly an early form of Chinese. Many characters are still recognisable today.
A queen who led armies

In 1976 archaeologists found the untouched tomb of Fu Hao , a wife of King Wu Ding. It held bronze weapons, jade and hundreds of bronzes. Oracle bones name her as a general who led thousands of soldiers. Women of this era could be powerful, though this was not the case later.
The big rebellion

About 1046 BCE , the Zhou people, from the west, defeated the last Shang king at the battle of Muye . The date is debated; various scholars say 1045 to 1027 BCE. The Zhou needed to explain why they could overthrow a king. They invented a political idea that would last 3,000 years.
The Mandate of Heaven
This is the Mandate of Heaven ( tianming ). It gave rulers authority but also a warning: rule badly and you can be overthrown. Chinese emperors used it for the next 3,000 years.
How true is the story?

Some historians suspect the Mandate was made up after the fact to justify the Zhou conquest. Others think it was sincere. Also, a famous story says a scholar, Wang Yirong, discovered oracle bones in 1899 when he saw 'dragon bones' in a pharmacy. Historians doubt parts of that tale. What is solid: the bones were being ground into medicine and the finds revealed Shang writing.

The Bronze Age Collapse of 1177 BCE
In a few decades, half the civilised world went dark

Around 1200 BCE, the Mediterranean world was a rich, connected network of kingdoms: Egypt, the Hittites, Mycenaean Greece, Ugarit, Babylon. Within about 50 years, most of them were ruined. The archaeologist Eric Cline called it the year civilisation collapsed in his 2014 book, 1177 B.C.
The golden age before the crash

The Late Bronze Age was globalised. Copper came from Cyprus. Tin came from far away, perhaps from today's Afghanistan or Central Asia. Kings wrote to each other as 'brother'. A shipwreck found off Uluburun (Turkey), about 1320 BCE, carried tonnes of copper and tin, ivory, glass and goods from many lands.
The last letters
At Ugarit, clay tablets baked by the fire that destroyed the city preserve a letter. The king said enemy ships had come, his army and fleet were elsewhere, and the land was left helpless.
Who were the Sea Peoples?

Egyptian carvings of Ramesses III (about 1177 BCE) show battles in the Nile Delta with foreign warriors in strange horned helmets and feather headdresses. Egypt called them 'Sea Peoples'. Nobody knows exactly who they were. Names like Peleset (maybe the Philistines) appear. Some may have been refugees, not just raiders.
A perfect storm

Evidence suggests drought and famine, earthquakes, internal revolts, and the breakdown of trade. When tin stopped, bronze was hard to make. A chain reaction followed, as the kingdoms depended on each other. Egypt survived but was weakened. The Hittites vanished. Greece lost writing for centuries (the Linear B script disappeared).
What came next

From the ruins came new things: iron became common, the alphabet spread, and new small states appeared, such as Israel, Phoenician cities and Aramaean kingdoms. Greece entered what is often called a Dark Age. But from it the city-states of classical Greece would later grow.
One cause or many?

Older books blamed the Sea Peoples alone. Most historians now say it was a system collapse : many causes interacting. Some stress climate. Others stress politics. Some say 'collapse' is too strong, since many places continued. The 'earthquake storm' idea, a run of earthquakes, is also disputed. No single explanation convinces everyone.

The Phoenicians and the Alphabet
A tiny people who sold purple, sailed everywhere and gave us ABC

Phoenicia was a string of port cities on the coast of today's Lebanon: Tyre, Sidon, Byblos. No big empire. Just clever merchants with fast ships. Their greatest export was not a thing you could hold. It was a way of writing.
The purple people

Phoenicians made a dye from the murex sea snail . It took thousands of snails to dye one garment. The colour, Tyrian purple, became the mark of kings and later of Roman emperors. The Greek name Phoinikes may come from the word for 'red' or 'purple'. The Phoenicians called themselves after their cities.
The alphabet

Before this, writing needed hundreds of signs (cuneiform, hieroglyphs). The Phoenician script had just 22 letters , each standing for a consonant. Anyone could learn it in days. It developed about 1050 BCE from earlier scripts used by Semitic speakers in Egypt and Canaan (the Proto-Sinaitic script, about 1800 BCE).
Greeks added the vowels
About 800 BCE the Greeks borrowed it and used some letters for vowels. The first two letters, aleph and beth , became alpha and beta , giving us the word 'alphabet'.
Sailors and colonists

Phoenician ships went across the Mediterranean and out to Spain and Atlantic Africa. They founded Cadiz in Spain and Carthage in North Africa. Tradition says Carthage was founded about 814 BCE by Queen Dido , who fled from Tyre. Dido is a legend; Carthage is real. Herodotus said a Phoenician crew sailed round Africa for the Egyptian Pharaoh Necho II (around 600 BCE). Historians still debate whether that happened.
The Carthage chapter

Carthage grew into a mighty sea power. It fought three wars against Rome, the Punic Wars (264-146 BCE). The great general Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants in 218 BCE. In 146 BCE, Rome destroyed Carthage. 'Punic' is simply the Latin word for Phoenician.
Did the Romans pour salt on Carthage?

Myth: Rome sowed Carthage's fields with salt so nothing would grow. Fact: there is no ancient source for it. The salt story appears in the 19th and 20th centuries. Rome did destroy the city and enslave its people, which is bad enough without the legend.

Persia: The First World Empire
A king who was told to be kind to conquered people

In 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great rode into Babylon, the biggest city in the world. The people did not fight him. Some cheered. How do you take a city without a war? The answer says a lot about how the Persians built the largest empire the world had yet seen.
From a small kingdom to everything

Cyrus came from Persis (today's Fars, Iran). Around 550 BCE he beat the Medes, then Lydia's rich king Croesus, then Babylon in 539 BCE . His son Cambyses added Egypt in 525 BCE. This was the Achaemenid Empire , named after an ancestor, Achaemenes.
Darius organises it

Darius I (ruled 522-486 BCE) split the empire into provinces run by governors called satraps . He built the Royal Road , about 2,500 km from Sardis to Susa, with relay stations for messengers. Standard coins and weights helped trade.
A message carved on a cliff

At Behistun in Iran, Darius had a giant relief carved about 520 BCE. It tells how he won the throne, in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. In the 1800s, scholars such as Henry Rawlinson used it to decipher cuneiform, much like the Rosetta Stone did for hieroglyphs.
Kind rule, strong rule

Persian kings let people keep their own religions and laws as long as they paid tribute. Cyrus is credited in the Bible (Book of Ezra) with letting Jews in Babylon return to Jerusalem. They also worshipped Ahura Mazda. Their faith is often tied to the prophet Zoroaster , whose dates are very uncertain.
Greece stands in the way

Persia clashed with Greek cities. At Marathon (490 BCE) Athens beat a Persian force. In 480 BCE Xerxes invaded with a huge army and fleet. The Greeks held at Thermopylae and then won at Salamis . Persia remained powerful for another 150 years until Alexander arrived.
Was the Cyrus Cylinder the first human rights charter?

The Cyrus Cylinder is a clay barrel, now in the British Museum. It says Cyrus restored gods to their temples and let displaced people go home. Some call it the first charter of human rights. Many historians disagree. It was a standard royal boast written to win over Babylon. It shows good policy, but not modern rights. Historians argue about how to read it.

The Axial Age: Buddha, Confucius, Socrates
Why did great thinkers pop up everywhere at once?

Between about 800 and 200 BCE, in India, China, Greece and Iran, people began to ask: how should we live? What is a good ruler? What happens after death? The German philosopher Karl Jaspers noticed this in 1949 and called it the Axial Age , a hinge of history.
The prince who walked out

Siddhartha Gautama , later the Buddha, was born in a Shakya clan family in Lumbini. His dates are debated: traditionally about 563-483 BCE, but many scholars now place his death between 410 and 400 BCE. According to tradition, he left home to seek an end to suffering. After years of search, he awakened at Bodh Gaya and taught the Middle Way, between luxury and extreme self-denial.
The teacher who wanted good order

Confucius (551-479 BCE) lived in a time when China's states were fighting. He taught that peace comes from good behaviour, respect for family and rulers who set an example. His sayings were collected by students in the Analects . He was not a success in his lifetime. He never got the high office he hoped for.
The man who only asked questions

Socrates (470-399 BCE) wrote nothing. We know him from Plato and Xenophon. He walked around Athens asking people to explain what they claimed to know, and embarrassed many. In 399 BCE an Athenian jury of 500 found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the young. He drank hemlock.
Others of the same age

In India, the Upanishads and the Jain teacher Mahavira (traditionally 6th century BCE) appeared. In China, Laozi (a possibly legendary figure) is linked with the Daodejing. In Iran, Zoroaster taught about good and evil. In Israel, prophets such as Isaiah wrote. None of them seems to have known the others.
Why then?
Ideas proposed: iron tools, growing trade, bigger states and cities, and cruel wars made people search for meaning. Money and writing helped ideas to spread. But nothing proves any single cause.
Was there really an 'age'?

Critics say the Axial Age is neat but artificial. The 'age' stretches 600 years. Egypt and Mesopotamia are left out. And many ideas had earlier roots. Also, a famous slip: the Buddha is sometimes called 'Indian-born'. Lumbini is in present-day Nepal . An inscription on an Ashokan pillar there, from about 249 BCE, says Ashoka visited the Buddha's birthplace.

Five things to remember Jaspers coined 'Axial Age' in 1949. Buddha, Confucius and Socrates were near-contemporaries in different places. Socrates wrote nothing and was executed in 399 BCE. The Axial Age idea is debated. Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace, is in Nepal. Think about it Would these thinkers have survived today's social media? Why do big questions arise in unsettled times?
Athens and Sparta
Two cities, two crazy ways to live

Athens gave us democracy, theatre and philosophy. Sparta gave us a state where boys were taken from their mothers at seven to become soldiers. They fought together against Persia. Then they fought each other for 27 years.
Athens invents voting

In 508/507 BCE, a reformer called Cleisthenes reorganised Athens so ordinary citizens shared power. The Assembly met on a hill, the Pnyx. Any male citizen could speak and vote. Many officials were picked by lottery . Citizens could also vote to exile a leader for ten years. This was ostracism , named after the pottery shards used as ballots.
But who counted?
Only adult male citizens voted. Women, slaves and foreigners did not. Perhaps 30,000-40,000 men could vote in a population of several hundred thousand. Athens was a democracy for a minority.
Sparta, the barracks state

Spartan boys entered the agoge at about seven. They trained, went hungry and learned to endure. Adults were full-time soldiers. Who grew the food? The helots , enslaved Greeks the Spartans ruled by terror. Spartans lived in constant fear of a helot revolt. Spartan women had more freedom than Athenian women, including owning land.
Heroes and a golden age

In 480 BCE King Leonidas of Sparta held the narrow pass at Thermopylae against Xerxes's huge army and died with his men. After Persia's defeat, Athens grew rich and built the Parthenon (447-432 BCE) under the leader Pericles .
27 years of war
The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) ended in Athens's defeat. A plague in Athens killed Pericles. The historian Thucydides wrote the war's history.
Did 300 Spartans stand alone at Thermopylae?

Myth: only 300 Spartans fought Persia. Fact: they were joined by several thousand other Greeks, including about 700 from Thespiae. Herodotus gives numbers around 7,000. Also, a favourite tale says Spartans threw weak babies off a cliff. The source is Plutarch, writing centuries later. A 2007 study of the supposed site found only adult remains.

Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Cleisthenes created Athenian democracy around 508 BCE. Only male citizens voted. Sparta used helots and trained boys in the agoge. The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) ended with Sparta's win. India had gana-sanghas at the same time. Think about it Can a democracy rest on slavery? Which is more admirable: Athens's openness or Sparta's discipline?
Alexander the Great
He conquered the world by 32 and then his army said no more

Alexander of Macedon became king at 20 and died at 32. In between, he marched about 20,000 km, defeated the mighty Persian Empire and reached the edge of India. Why did he stop? And how did he die? Read on.
The boy from Pella

Alexander was born in 356 BCE in Pella, Macedon. His father, Philip II , had built a mighty army. His tutor was the philosopher Aristotle . He tamed the wild horse Bucephalus as a boy. In 336 BCE Philip was assassinated and Alexander became king.
Beating Persia
Alexander's army was small but skilled and he led from the front. At Gaugamela (331 BCE) he beat a much larger Persian force. He took Babylon and Susa, and burned Persepolis in 330 BCE.
To the end of the known world

He marched through Afghanistan and Central Asia, and into the Punjab. In 326 BCE, at the river Hydaspes (Jhelum), he defeated King Porus . Greek writers say he was so impressed that he gave Porus's land back. Then, at the river Hyphasis (Beas), his weary soldiers refused to go on. After years of fighting, they wanted to go home.
Death in Babylon

Alexander died on about 10-11 June 323 BCE, in Babylon, aged 32, after a fever of about ten days. Causes debated: typhoid, malaria, alcohol, poison. Many theories, no proof. Asked who should inherit, he supposedly said, 'to the strongest'. Historians doubt it. His generals, the Diadochi , split the empire. Ptolemy took Egypt, Seleucus most of Asia.
What he left behind

Alexander founded many cities named Alexandria. The one in Egypt became a centre of learning. Greek language and culture spread across Asia, giving the 'Hellenistic' world. He also left chaos, destruction and thousands dead. Admirers and critics have fought about him for 2,000 years.
Did he conquer India?

Myth: Alexander conquered India. Fact: he reached the Punjab, the north-west edge, and spent about two years there. He turned back. No Indian source records him by name. Greek writers are our main evidence. It is true he never lost a major battle, but Hydaspes was costly, and his men were exhausted.

The vacuum that Chandragupta filled
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Alexander ruled Macedon from 336 and died in 323 BCE. He beat Persia at Issus and Gaugamela. At the Hydaspes (326 BCE) he beat Porus. His death is unexplained. The Mauryas rose soon after. Think about it Is 'the Great' the right title for him? Why might Indian sources not mention him?
Rome: From Republic to Empire
A republic that hated kings ended up with an emperor

Rome began as a small town on the Tiber. Legend says it was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus, who killed his twin Remus. Legend is fun, but the real story is better. Five centuries later Romans swore they would never again live under a king. Then they did, just with a different name.
No more kings

Tradition says Rome's last king, Tarquin the Proud, was thrown out in 509 BCE . Romans set up a Republic ( res publica , 'public thing'). Two consuls , elected for one year, led the state. A Senate of elders advised. Ordinary citizens (the plebs) won their own officials, the tribunes.
Empire by war

Rome beat its Italian neighbours, then fought Carthage in the Punic Wars (264-146 BCE) and destroyed it. It took Greece, Spain and more. The spoils enriched a few and ruined many farmers. Rich generals with loyal armies became dangerous. The system strained.
Caesar crosses a river

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, then in 49 BCE crossed the Rubicon with his army, an act of war against Rome. He won the civil war and became dictator. On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE , senators stabbed him, led by Brutus and Cassius.
The quiet takeover

Caesar's heir Octavian beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus . He never called himself king. He kept the Senate and the offices, but held real power. This began the Pax Romana , about two centuries of relative peace and prosperity.
Life in the empire

At its height under Trajan (117 CE), Rome stretched from Britain to Syria. Roads, aqueducts and one law linked millions. Latin and Greek were everywhere. But around half the people in Italy might have been enslaved, and gladiator games were mass entertainment. Rome was impressive and brutal at once.
What did Caesar's death really look like?

Myth 1: Caesar said 'Et tu, Brute?' That line is Shakespeare's (1599). Ancient writers disagree about his last words; Suetonius records one version in Greek. Myth 2: the Caesarean section is named after Caesar's birth. His mother lived long after, and such operations then were nearly always fatal for the mother. The name probably comes from the Latin word for cut.

Five things to remember The Republic began about 509 BCE. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and died in 44 BCE. Augustus became first emperor in 27 BCE. Rome and India traded heavily. Think about it Why do republics fall when armies are loyal to generals? Was Augustus a saviour or a trickster?
Han China and the Silk Road
A man went to find allies and came back 13 years later

In about 138 BCE, the Han emperor Wu sent an officer named Zhang Qian west to find allies against the Xiongnu, the horse-riding nomads who kept raiding China. The Xiongnu captured him. He escaped after about ten years, kept going, and came home after thirteen. He had opened up the world.
From Qin to Han

In 221 BCE Qin Shi Huang united China and was buried with a clay army. His dynasty fell fast. In 202 BCE, Liu Bang , a commoner, founded the Han dynasty, which ruled until 220 CE. Han rulers used Confucian ideas for their officials. Emperor Wu (141-87 BCE) expanded the empire a lot.
Zhang Qian's report

Zhang Qian reported on cities, horses and peoples in Central Asia, such as Ferghana's famous horses and a land called Daxia (Bactria). The Han then pushed into the Tarim basin. Trade followed. Chinese silk, so light and so valuable, travelled west. Horses, grapes and glass came east.
A road with no name
There was no single 'Silk Road'. The name was coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. Few travellers went the whole way. Goods passed through many hands and prices soared.
Ideas, paper and plague

Han China made big advances: paper (a court official, Cai Lun, presented an improved paper in 105 CE), the seismoscope of Zhang Heng, and a census in 2 CE counting about 58 million people. Along with silk, the road carried religions and diseases. Large epidemics are recorded in both empires in the 2nd century CE.
Han meets Rome (almost)

In 97 CE a Han envoy, Gan Ying , got as far as the Persian Gulf but turned back, scared by stories of a long sea voyage. Chinese records mention a 'Daqin' (Rome) embassy in 166 CE, probably merchants. The two empires knew about each other but never really met.
Was the Silk Road mainly about silk?

Myth: it carried mostly silk from China to Rome. Fact: it carried everything: spices, horses, glass, gold, ideas and religions. Buddhism, Manichaeism and later Islam travelled. Also, sea routes were big too, especially to India and Rome. Finally, Rome's elite loved silk so much that some senators objected. That is true.

Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Han (202 BCE-220 CE) followed the short-lived Qin. Zhang Qian's journey opened Central Asia to China. The Silk Road was a web, not one road. Paper, census and science marked the Han. Kushans linked India to the Silk Road. Think about it Why would empires fight to control trade routes? What travels faster along trade routes, goods or ideas?
The Fall of Rome (and Why It Didn't Really Fall)
The last emperor was a teenager named after Rome's first king and first emperor

In 476 CE, the last western Roman emperor was a boy called Romulus Augustulus . That name mixes Romulus, the legendary founder, and Augustus, the first emperor. 'Augustulus' means 'little Augustus'. He was deposed, retired to a comfortable villa, and nobody much noticed. So did Rome fall that day?
Trouble for centuries
In the 3rd century CE, civil wars, plagues and invasions nearly broke the empire. Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople in 330 CE. After 395 CE, the empire was usually ruled in two halves.
The Huns push, the Goths cross

The Huns, horse-riders from Central Asia, drove Goths into Roman land in 376 CE. In 378, at Adrianople , the Goths killed Emperor Valens and destroyed a Roman army. Barbarians were not new. Rome had hired them for years. But now whole peoples were settling inside the borders.
Rome is sacked

In 410 CE the Visigoth king Alaric entered Rome and plundered it for three days. It was the first time in about 800 years that the city had fallen to an enemy. The shock rang across the world. In 455 the Vandals sacked it again. By then, the western emperors were often puppets of generals.
The quiet end

In 476, a general called Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and sent the royal regalia to the eastern emperor in Constantinople. He ruled Italy as a king. The Eastern Roman Empire (later called Byzantine) carried on for almost 1,000 more years, until 1453.
Why? The great argument

Edward Gibbon ( The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire , 1776-89) blamed barbarians and also Christianity, which he said sapped the old Roman spirit. Modern historians often look at wars, taxes, plague, climate and politics together. There is no single answer.
Fall or transformation?

Peter Brown and others call this period late antiquity , a time of change more than collapse. Roman law, Latin and the Church survived under new kings. Others disagree. Bryan Ward-Perkins argued in 2005 that it was a catastrophe: trade shrank, pottery got worse, cities shrank. Archaeology supports him in places like Britain.

Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Rome's troubles were centuries long. Alaric sacked Rome in 410 CE. 476 CE ended the Western line. The East lasted until 1453. Historians argue between 'fall' and 'transformation'. Think about it Did a society really end, or just change its rulers? What lessons might this hold for modern states?
Carthage and Hannibal: The Enemy Rome Almost Lost To
The city that nearly ruled the Mediterranean

For a long time Rome was one city-state among many. Its real test came from Carthage, a sea power in North Africa with ports across the western Mediterranean. Between 264 and 146 BCE the two states fought three wars. The second one nearly ended with Hannibal marching into Italy. What would Europe look like if he had won?
A city founded by traders

Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded Carthage, in today's Tunisia. Later Roman writers dated it to 814 BCE, though the date is a tradition, not proof. Carthage grew rich on trade in metal, purple dye and grain. It held Sicily, Sardinia and much of Spain. Its navy was feared and its merchants sailed far beyond the Strait of Gibraltar.
The First Punic War over Sicily

The name Punic comes from the Latin word for Phoenician. The first war (264–241 BCE) was fought over Sicily. Rome built a fleet from scratch and beat Carthage at sea. Carthage lost Sicily and had to pay a huge sum. Its general Hamilcar Barca then turned to Spain, and he raised a new army there for his family.
Polybius and a boy's oath

Polybius (c. 200–118 BCE) A Greek who was held as a hostage in Rome, Polybius wrote the Histories , the best surviving account of the wars. He says that Hannibal, as a child, swore an oath at his father's altar to be an enemy of Rome. Polybius is not neutral. He wanted to explain why Rome had become master of the Mediterranean, so read him with care.
Five dates that shaped the war
Hannibal led his army from Spain, over the Alps, into northern Italy in 218 BCE, with a few dozen war elephants. Most of them did not survive the cold.
Cannae, the battle taught in military schools

In 216 BCE, at Cannae in southern Italy, Hannibal set up a curved line that gave way in the centre and then closed round the Roman army. The Romans lost tens of thousands of men in a single day. Many later generals studied Cannae as a model of encirclement. Hannibal still could not take Rome itself. Its allies stayed loyal, and Rome refused to make peace.
Scipio takes the fight to Africa

Rome's general Scipio decided to attack Carthage directly. He landed in North Africa and forced Hannibal home from Italy. At Zama in 202 BCE Scipio defeated him, and the Second Punic War ended. Scipio took the name Africanus. Carthage gave up its navy and most of its empire, and it had to pay Rome a large indemnity over 50 years.
Did Rome sow salt on Carthage?

A popular story says the Romans sowed the fields of Carthage with salt so nothing would grow again. It is a dramatic image, and many people repeat it. Most historians doubt it. The sources are late and vague, and Roman writers did not agree on it. Rome did destroy Carthage in 146 BCE, but the salt story is probably a later legend. Historians argue how far the destruction went.
Which pass did Hannibal use?

Scholars still debate the route of Hannibal's army over the Alps. Possible passes include the Little St Bernard, the Col de la Seigne and the Col du Clapier. Each theory has supporters. Some use landscape and timing, others use the words of ancient writers. The debate shows how hard it is to rebuild a march that happened more than two thousand years ago.
The last war and the end of Carthage

Hannibal went into exile and died in the 180s BCE at the court of King Prusias of Bithynia, in Asia Minor. Carthage slowly rebuilt its trade and its wealth. Rome grew nervous about its rival. In 149 BCE it began the Third Punic War. After a siege of about three years, Carthage fell in 146 BCE, and Rome turned the land into a province called Africa.
Meanwhile in India…

When Zama was fought in 202 BCE, the Mauryan empire in India was breaking up. Ashoka had died about 232 BCE. In 185 BCE the Shunga dynasty took power in Magadha. Within about twenty years, Greek kings from Bactria would rule parts of north-west India, and their coins carried both Greek and Indian scripts. The Mediterranean and Indian worlds were already touching.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Three Punic Wars were fought between Rome and Carthage from 264 to 146 BCE. Hannibal crossed the Alps in 218 BCE and won at Cannae in 216 BCE. Scipio beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE. Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE. Polybius is our key source, and he was biased toward Rome. Think about it Why did Rome keep going after a defeat that would have ended most states? How much of the 'salt on the fields' story is memory and how much is propaganda?
The Sasanian Empire: Rome's Eternal Rival
Rome's longest rival

For four centuries, from about 224 to 651 CE, Rome and Persia were the two great powers of the west. They fought over Armenia, Mesopotamia and the trade routes between them. The Sasanian Empire is less famous than Rome, but its story shows how a state can rise, fight a superpower, and then fall to a new faith and a new army.
Ardashir takes the crown

Ardashir came from Persis, the homeland of the old Persian kings. Around 224 CE he defeated the last Parthian king and took over the Iranian plateau. He claimed descent from a priest called Sasan. He built his capital at Ctesiphon, on the Tigris near modern Baghdad. Ardashir tied kingship to the religion of Zoroaster, and a priest named Kartir carved long texts praising the faith on rock walls.
A Roman emperor in chains

In 260 CE Shapur I, Ardashir's son, defeated the Roman army at Edessa and captured the emperor Valerian. This was an enormous humiliation for Rome, the first time a reigning emperor was taken prisoner. A rock relief at Naqsh-e Rustam shows Shapur on horseback, with Valerian kneeling before him. Persian kings used art like this to show their power to everyone who passed by.
Khosrow I and the state

Khosrow I Anushirvan (ruled 531–579) Khosrow reformed taxes, the army and the land survey. Later Persian writers remembered him as the model of a just king. He made peace with Justinian in 562, a treaty known as the Fifty Years' Peace. The peace was meant to last half a century. It broke down after about ten years, which tells you how fragile these deals were.
Key dates of the empire
The empire lasted about four hundred years. Its last king died in exile in the east, while Arab armies took the western heartland.
The trade of the Persian Gulf

The Sasanians controlled the Persian Gulf and much of the sea route to India and China. Persian merchants sold silk, spices and horses. Sogdian traders from Central Asia worked closely with them. Ports on the Gulf coast were busy. Ships carried goods between Iraq, Iran and the Indian coast, so the empire earned a lot from tolls and taxes on trade.
Were Rome and Persia always at war?

Many textbooks show Rome and Persia as eternal enemies. The image of two giants fighting for centuries is easy to remember. Historians argue this is too simple. There were long periods of diplomacy, gift-giving and trade. The wars were mostly about buffer kingdoms like Armenia, and both sides often accepted peace when it suited them.
The last great war

Khosrow II, a grandson of Khosrow I, won huge gains in the early 600s. Persian armies took Jerusalem in 614 and carried off the relic of the True Cross. The emperor Heraclius struck back, invaded Persia and defeated its army near Nineveh in 627. Khosrow II was overthrown and killed in 628. Both empires were badly drained by the long war.
A new power from the desert

After 632 the Arab armies of the new Islamic state moved fast. They defeated the exhausted Sasanian forces at Qadisiyya and took Ctesiphon. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed in 651 at Merv while on the run. Historians still debate how easily the Arabs conquered the empire. Some say the Sasanian state was already weakened by civil wars and tax revolts. Others stress the speed of the Arab advance.
Legacy in stone and story

The brick vault of the Taq Kasra at Ctesiphon is one of the great surviving arches of the ancient world. Its ruins still stand beside the Tigris. Later Persian writers, including Ferdowsi in the Shahnameh (around 1010), kept Sasanian royal stories alive. Iranian national memory still draws on this era more than on the centuries that followed.
Meanwhile in India…

Khosrow I's court welcomed ideas from India. Indian animal fables were translated into Middle Persian as Kalila wa Dimna. The game of chaturanga also reached Persia, where it became shatranj, the ancestor of chess. Persian and Indian merchants shared the same sea. Persian ships traded with the ports of western India, and the cultural exchange ran both ways.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Sasanian Empire ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from 224 to 651 CE. Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian in 260 CE. Khosrow I made the Fifty Years' Peace with Justinian in 562. Zoroastrianism was closely tied to the state. The Arab conquests ended the dynasty in the 650s. Think about it Why did long wars with Rome leave both empires weaker? How did trade across the Gulf make Persia rich?
Byzantium: The Empire That Lasted 1,000 Years
The Romans who never called themselves Byzantine

The empire we call Byzantine never used that name. Its people called themselves Romans right until the end. The word 'Byzantine' was popularised by a German scholar, Hieronymus Wolf, in 1557, more than a century after the empire fell. So the Roman Empire did not die in 476 CE. It simply moved east and lived another thousand years.
A capital on a strait

In 330 CE Constantine made the old Greek town of Byzantium into Constantinople , the 'city of Constantine'. It sat where Europe meets Asia, controlling sea trade between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. The huge Theodosian Walls (built in the 5th century) kept the city safe for about a thousand years.
Justinian and Theodora

Justinian ruled 527-565 CE. His wife Theodora , a former actress, was a real partner in power. In 532 the Nika riots nearly toppled him. Legend says Theodora stopped him fleeing by saying that royalty is a fine burial shroud. Thousands of rioters died. He rebuilt Hagia Sophia in five years (finished 537), still dazzling today, and ordered a clear collection of Roman law, the Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534), which shaped European law.
Fire on water
The Byzantines used Greek fire , a burning liquid sprayed from ships, even burning on water. The exact recipe has been lost.
Wounds from friends

In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, supposedly heading to Egypt, attacked Constantinople instead and plundered it. The Byzantines retook it in 1261 but never fully recovered. A new power, the Ottomans, closed in.
The last day

On 29 May 1453 , Sultan Mehmed II took the city after a siege. His big cannons, designed by a Hungarian engineer called Orban, shattered the walls. The last emperor, Constantine XI , died fighting. The Ottomans turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque. Many scholars fled to Italy with Greek books, helping to fuel the Renaissance.
Was 'Byzantine' just about plots and complexity?

Myth: 'Byzantine' means a mess of intrigue. Fact: the word became an insult in the 18th century (Enlightenment writers like Gibbon and Montesquieu looked down on it). The empire actually ran an efficient tax system, a strong navy and excellent diplomacy. Also, they spoke Greek, not Latin, from about the 7th century. Yet they never stopped calling themselves Roman.

Five things to remember Byzantium was the Roman Empire in the east. Justinian built Hagia Sophia and codified law. The walls and Greek fire saved the city for centuries. The Fourth Crusade struck it in 1204. It fell to the Ottomans on 29 May 1453. Think about it Why is the name 'Byzantine' misleading? What survives of Rome in the East?
The Rise of Islam and the Abbasid Golden Age
From a desert town to the world's best library in 200 years

In about 610 CE, a merchant of Mecca named Muhammad began to preach. Within a century, an Arabic-speaking empire stretched from Spain to Sindh. How did this happen so fast? And what did it do with the world's books once it got them?
The beginning

Muhammad (about 570-632 CE) taught belief in one God. After conflict in Mecca, he moved to Medina in 622 CE , the Hijra. That year begins the Islamic calendar. By his death most of Arabia was united. The next leaders, the Rashidun caliphs, conquered Syria, Egypt and Persia in about 30 years. The Persian and Byzantine empires were exhausted from wars with each other.
The Umayyads, then a revolution

The Umayyad caliphate (661-750) ruled from Damascus. Arabs held top posts, and non-Arab converts resented it. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads, with strong support from Persian-speaking eastern regions. One Umayyad prince escaped and founded a state in Spain.
A circular city
Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 as a round city on the Tigris. It became one of the largest cities in the world, with a paper industry (the craft came from China) feeding its book markets.
Scholars of the golden age

Al-Khwarizmi (about 780-850) wrote a book on al-jabr , giving us 'algebra'. His name gives us 'algorithm'. Ibn al-Haytham (about 965-1040) did experiments on light and sight. Al-Razi wrote on medicine. Al-Biruni studied India. The House of Wisdom in Baghdad is famous as a great library and translation centre. Historians disagree on how formal it really was.
The end of the golden age

Abbasid power weakened as regional rulers took over. In 1258, the Mongol army of Hulagu sacked Baghdad and killed the last Abbasid caliph. Many people died; estimates vary widely. But Islamic science and culture lived on in Cairo, Cordoba, Samarkand and later in Istanbul and Delhi.
Did the Tigris run black with ink?

Myth: in 1258 the Tigris ran black with the ink of books thrown in by the Mongols, and red with blood. Fact: this poetic image comes from later writers. Baghdad's libraries were badly damaged, but exact details are uncertain. Also, 'Arabic numerals' are a misnomer: Arabs got them from India.

Numbers, zero and the sword
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Hijra in 622 marks year one of the Islamic calendar. The Umayyads (661-750) ruled from Damascus; the Abbasids from Baghdad. Baghdad's scholars saved and extended world knowledge. Al-Khwarizmi gave us algebra and algorithm. The Mongols took Baghdad in 1258. Think about it What makes a city a centre of knowledge? Who deserves credit for an idea that travels through many hands?
Tang and Song China: The Medieval Superpower
China had the world's best inventions 500 years before Europe caught up

Imagine a world city of one million people in 750 CE, with poets, parties and foreign merchants. That was Chang'an , capital of the Tang. A few centuries later, China's Song era produced printing, paper money and gunpowder weapons. Let us meet them.
The Tang (618-907)

After a short Sui dynasty, Li Yuan founded the Tang in 618. His son Li Shimin (Emperor Taizong) was a strong ruler. The empire's capital Chang'an drew traders from Persia, Central Asia and Japan. Tang poets Li Bai and Du Fu are still loved. Wu Zetian ruled as China's only female emperor (690-705).
A rebellion shakes the Tang
In 755 General An Lushan rebelled. The war lasted until 763 and killed millions or left them uncounted; Tang rule never fully recovered. Provincial governors grew stronger. The dynasty ended in 907.
Song inventions
The Song (960-1279) had a booming economy: iron output, cities, banknotes, and ships with compasses. The oldest dated printed book is the Diamond Sutra of 868 , found at Dunhuang.
Scholars and civil servants

The Song relied heavily on civil service exams . Aspiring officials studied Confucian classics. It was a rare chance, though most successful candidates came from well-off families. Capital Kaifeng was crowded, with night markets. The Song fell back to the south after the Jurchen took the north in 1127. The Southern Song lasted till the Mongols in 1279.
Women and foot-binding

Foot-binding began in the Song era among elites, and later spread. It hurt women for centuries. The Song also saw the rise of Neo-Confucianism, which put more rules on women's lives. Progress had a hard side.
Did the Chinese invent gunpowder for fireworks?

Myth: it was a toy. Fact: it was found by alchemists looking for medicines, probably in the Tang era. Early Song texts such as the Wujing Zongyao (1044) list recipes for military use, and the Song used bombs and fire-arrows. Historians also argue about a Song 'industrial revolution' (Mark Elvin's 'medieval economic revolution'). It did not lead to machines like Britain's later one.
