Pilgrims and ships
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Tang (618-907) had a cosmopolitan capital, Chang'an. The An Lushan rebellion (755-763) weakened the Tang. The Song (960-1279) saw printing, paper money, gunpowder and the compass in use. Civil service exams selected officials. India and China exchanged monks, envoys and trade. Think about it Why might invention not always lead to an industrial revolution? What does Chang'an tell you about being open to the world?
The Crusades: Holy War and Holy Trade
Holy war with a price tag

The Crusades lasted, on and off, from 1095 to the 1290s. They shaped how Europe and the Muslim world saw each other, and their memory is still used in politics today. People went on Crusade for faith, for land, for money and for fame. Most of them were not thinking about the long-term effects. Those effects reached far beyond the Holy Land.
A pope calls for a holy war

In November 1095 Pope Urban II spoke at Clermont in France. He asked knights to free the Christians of the East and take Jerusalem. Those who went and died, he promised, would have their sins forgiven. A large crowd roared the answer, "God wills it." Preachers such as Peter the Hermit led a popular movement. Some of these groups attacked Jewish communities along the Rhine in 1096, a terrible episode that shows the violence the call could unleash.
Jerusalem falls in 1099

The main crusader army reached Jerusalem in 1099 after a long march through Anatolia and Syria. It took the city in July after a short siege, and chroniclers describe a massacre of its Muslim and Jewish residents. The crusaders set up states along the coast and inland: Jerusalem, Antioch, Edessa and Tripoli. Europeans called them the Outremer, or land beyond the sea. They lasted for almost two centuries.
Usama ibn Munqidh and the Franks

Usama ibn Munqidh (1095–1188) A Syrian noble and warrior, Usama wrote a memoir called Kitab al-I'tibar (The Book of Contemplation). He describes Frankish knights as rough and proud, but he also records friendships and cases where Franks showed him courtesy. His book reminds us that the Crusades were lived by ordinary people on both sides. It was not just one story of good against evil.
Crusades and counter-crusades
The Crusades were not one war. They were a long series of campaigns, sieges and truces, fought by armies that changed every few years.
Saladin and Richard

In 1187 Saladin defeated the crusader army at the Horns of Hattin and then took Jerusalem. Europe was shocked, and the Third Crusade (1189–1192) was called to win it back. Richard the Lionheart of England and Philip II of France led the army. Richard won some victories but never took Jerusalem. The Treaty of Jaffa in 1192 left the city in Muslim hands, though Christian pilgrims could visit it.
The Children's Crusade of 1212

A famous story tells of thousands of children who marched to Jerusalem in 1212, only to be sold into slavery or to die on the way. It is one of the most haunting tales of the medieval world. Historians argue about it. The sources are thin and written later. Some believe a real movement of young people happened, but the stories of mass child slavery look more like legend or moral warning. The debate is still open.
The Fourth Crusade turns on Christians

In 1204 the Fourth Crusade was meant to attack Egypt. But the crusaders were deep in debt to Venice, which wanted its own gains. They ended up storming Constantinople, a Christian city. The sack of Constantinople shocked the Byzantines. Treasures and relics were carried off to Venice and the West. A Latin empire ruled the city until 1261, and many Greeks never forgave the Latins for it.
Holy war, holy trade

Italian port cities like Venice and Genoa grew rich carrying crusaders and their supplies. They gained trading colonies in the eastern Mediterranean and new contacts with Arab and Byzantine merchants. Historians argue whether the Crusades were mainly religious or mainly economic. The best answer is that faith, power and profit were tangled together. Crusading ideas also influenced later wars in Spain and the Baltic.
Saladin's city after the war

Saladin treated Jerusalem with more restraint than the crusaders had shown in 1099. He allowed Christians to stay and, according to later accounts, he ransomed many prisoners at a low price. His reputation grew in Europe as well. Medieval writers made him into a model of chivalry, and his story became a favourite among later storytellers and poets.
Memory that outlived the armies

The last crusader stronghold, Acre, fell to the Mamluks in 1291. The crusading states were gone, but the memory of the Crusades lived on in art, literature and political language. In the modern world, the word "crusade" is used in political speeches on both sides. Historians now try to tell the story from many viewpoints, including those of Muslims, Byzantines and local Christians.
Meanwhile in India…

In 1192 Muhammad of Ghor defeated the Rajput ruler Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain, near Delhi. The victory opened the way for Turkish and Afghan rulers to set up a sultanate in Delhi. Qutb-ud-din Aibak, one of Muhammad's generals, became the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Across the world, the same century saw holy wars and new states spreading in different directions.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Pope Urban II launched the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095. The crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099. Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187. The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204. Acre fell in 1291, ending the crusader states. Think about it Were the Crusades a religious war, an economic one, or both? Why do Crusade stories still stir strong feelings today?
The Khmer Empire and Angkor's Water City
A city the size of a country

Angkor, in today's Cambodia, was one of the largest pre-industrial cities on Earth. Its temples, canals and reservoirs were built by the Khmer Empire between the 800s and the 1400s. Most of Angkor's people lived in wooden houses that have long since rotted away. What survives is stone, and stone can mislead us about how big the city really was.
A king who claimed the gods

Around 802 CE a young prince named Jayavarman II proclaimed himself a universal king on a mountain called Mahendraparvata, now Phnom Kulen. He created a royal cult, the devaraja, which tied the king to the god Shiva. The Khmer kings then built an empire that stretched across much of mainland Southeast Asia. Their power rested on rice, labour and water, and on Sanskrit culture that came by sea from India.
Angkor Wat, the temple of Vishnu

Suryavarman II (reigned about 1113 to 1150) built Angkor Wat, dedicated to the god Vishnu. It is one of the largest religious monuments in the world, surrounded by a moat about five kilometres around. Its walls carry long carved reliefs, including a procession of the king and scenes from Hindu epics. The temple was built as a model of the universe, with the central peak representing Mount Meru.
Zhou Daguan's eyewitness notes

Zhou Daguan (visit 1296–1297) A Chinese envoy sent to the Khmer court, Zhou wrote Customs of Cambodia . He describes markets, houses, clothes and the way people traded with Chinese merchants. He is our best eyewitness of Angkor at its height. His notes are short, but they show a busy city full of trade and daily life.
The Khmer story in five dates
The dates show a line from a new kingdom to a great temple state, and then to its slow decline and its loss to the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya.
Jayavarman VII and the hospitals

Jayavarman VII ruled around 1181 to about 1218. He built the great temple of the Bayon at the centre of Angkor Thom, with its towers of smiling faces, and he rebuilt much of the empire after wars with the Cham kingdom. Inscriptions say he founded many rest houses and hospitals, around a hundred of them, along the royal roads. Historians see this as a sign of a king who wanted to be seen as caring for the sick and travellers.
Water, the hidden engine

Angkor's kings dug huge reservoirs called barays. The East Baray was several kilometres long. They stored monsoon water for rice fields and for the dry season, and canals linked the city to the wider landscape. Water was power in Angkor. A king who could feed his people through the dry season could hold his followers together. Historians now treat the water system as one of the most impressive engineering feats of its age.
Did the jungle swallow Angkor?

A popular image shows Angkor overgrown by jungle, abandoned by a people who simply walked away. It made a great story when French explorers found the ruins in the 1860s. Historians argue the real story is more complex. Droughts, floods, shifting rivers, war with Ayutthaya and changing religion all played a part. The water system may have failed under extreme monsoon swings, but the causes are still debated.
The sack of 1431

In 1431 the armies of Ayutthaya, the Thai kingdom to the west, sacked Angkor. Much of the court moved south, and in the following decades the capital shifted towards what is now Phnom Penh. Angkor did not disappear. Monks kept the temples in use, and later kings were crowned there. But the royal city was no longer the centre of power.
Stone that survived the fall

Angkor Wat appears on the Cambodian flag, and the temple complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its stone carvings show the wide reach of Indian ideas in Southeast Asia. Modern Cambodians see Angkor as a source of national pride. Historians argue about how to present the story, since it was built by thousands of workers, many of them forced to labour for the state.
Meanwhile in India…

In about 1025 the Chola king Rajendra I sent a naval expedition across the Bay of Bengal. It attacked the ports of Srivijaya in Sumatra, the sea power that controlled much of the trade with the Khmer lands. The Khmer court took Sanskrit as its learned language, and its kings carved the Ramayana and Mahabharata into stone. Indian stories were part of the everyday culture of Angkor.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Khmer Empire grew from the early 800s. Angkor Wat was built for Vishnu under Suryavarman II. Zhou Daguan left the best eyewitness account of the city. Reservoirs (barays) were the engine of rice production. Ayutthaya sacked Angkor in 1431. Think about it How much of Angkor's fall came from nature, and how much from people? Why did a temple state need so many workers?
The Vikings
The monks of Lindisfarne had a very bad Monday

On 8 June 793, raiders in dragon-prowed ships landed at the monastery of Lindisfarne off England's coast. They killed monks and took treasure. The English scholar Alcuin wrote in shock that nothing like it had been seen. This is where the Viking Age begins, a 250-year burst of raids, trade and settlement from Scandinavia.
The ships

Their longships were light and shallow, and could cross open sea and sail up rivers. They had a sail and oars. A raiding party could appear from nowhere and leave quickly. 'Viking' meant to go raiding. Most Scandinavians were farmers, traders and craftspeople.
West and east

In the east, Swedish Vikings called the Rus travelled down rivers. Tradition says Rurik founded Novgorod around 862. They gave Russia its name. The Byzantine emperors hired them as the Varangian Guard .
Iceland's parliament

Settlers reached Iceland around 874. In 930 they set up the Althing , often called the world's oldest surviving parliament, where chiefs met to make laws. From Iceland came the great sagas. Erik the Red was exiled and founded a colony in Greenland about 985.
America, 500 years early

His son Leif Erikson reached North America about 1000 CE. At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, archaeologists found Norse buildings. A 2021 study of tree rings dated cut wood there to 1021 CE . The colony did not last. They probably clashed with local peoples and were too far from home.
1066 and the end

The Vikings settled in northern France, where they became the Normans . In 1066 two invasions hit England. King Harold beat the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, then lost to William of Normandy at Hastings. By then, Scandinavian kings had become Christian. The Viking Age faded.
Did Vikings wear horned helmets?

Myth: yes. Fact: no Viking helmet with horns has ever been found. The image comes from 19th-century costume art, especially for Wagner's operas (1876). Also, Vikings were not only raiders. They traded, farmed and settled, and some women owned property. A burial at Birka in Sweden once thought a male warrior was shown by DNA to be a woman (2017), though what that means is debated.
Meanwhile in India…
A Buddha in Sweden
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Viking Age started with Lindisfarne in 793. Longships let them raid and trade. Vikings reached Iceland, Greenland and North America. The Rus helped found early Russia. Horned helmets are a myth. Think about it Why did Scandinavians go overseas? Who counts as a 'Viking'?
Genghis Khan and the Mongol World
An orphan on the run built the largest land empire ever

The boy was called Temüjin . Born around 1162, he saw his father poisoned when he was a child. His family was left to starve on the steppe. He grew up to unite every Mongol tribe and in 1206 was named Genghis Khan ('Chinggis', a title whose exact meaning is debated).
From nobody to Khan

Temüjin survived by wits. His wife Börte was kidnapped and he rescued her. He used loyal friends rather than only family. His army was divided into groups of ten, hundred, thousand. Promotions went to the skilled, not just nobles. In 1206, a kurultai (assembly) proclaimed him ruler.
Terror and speed

Mongol armies were fast horse-archers who could ride very long distances. They used spies and tricks. Cities that fought could be wiped out. The Khwarazmian empire (Central Asia, 1219-1221) was ruined after its governor killed Mongol envoys or traders. Genghis died in 1227, while fighting Western Xia. His burial place has never been found.
His sons and grandsons

His grandson Batu reached Hungary in 1241, then withdrew when Great Khan Ogedei died (the exact reason is debated). Kublai Khan took all China and founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271. Hulagu took Baghdad in 1258.
The Mongol peace

The Mongols protected trade routes. A relay system, the yam , with riders and stations, carried messages. Travellers with a metal pass ( paiza ) got food and horses. This 'Pax Mongolica' let Marco Polo and others travel. The Mongols were mostly tolerant of religions, though they could be cruel.
Fragmentation

By the late 1200s the empire had split into four khanates. Yuan China fell in 1368. The Golden Horde ruled Russia for generations. At its peak the empire covered about 24 million square km, the biggest contiguous land empire in history.
Destroyer or builder?

Persian and Chinese sources describe massacres, with huge figures (sometimes millions) that modern historians doubt as exaggerated. A famous 2003 study found a Y-chromosome line shared by about 8 percent of men in a big region of Asia. It is linked to a single male ancestor around 1,000 years ago. Some say it may be Genghis Khan's family, but this is a guess and scholars are cautious.
Meanwhile in India…
The wall of the Indus
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Genghis Khan was proclaimed ruler in 1206. His army used merit, speed and discipline. The empire split into khanates among his heirs. The yam relay and the Pax Mongolica helped trade. Mongols turned back at the Indus in 1221. Think about it Should an empire be judged by its builders or its victims? Why would tolerance for religions help a conquering state?
The Black Death
The worst disaster in European history began with a sick ship

In October 1347, a few Genoese ships docked at Messina in Sicily. Many sailors were dead. Those alive were covered with black swellings that oozed. The port authorities ordered them out. Too late. The Black Death had arrived.
The road from Asia

The disease is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis , confirmed by DNA from plague-pit skeletons. It was usually spread by fleas on rats, though it could also spread from person to person in its lung form.
How bad?

Historians estimate that about a third to a half of Europeans died in 1347-1351. Estimates differ, and some areas were barely touched. Cities with crowded streets suffered most. In the Middle East and North Africa, too, millions died. Victims got fever, black swellings called buboes, and many died within days. Doctors had no cure. Many blamed bad air or the stars.
Panic and scapegoats

Some people whipped themselves in public, the Flagellants , hoping to please God. Others blamed Jews and attacked communities, for example in Strasbourg in 1349. The Pope condemned the violence, but it went on. By 1377 the port of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) required ships to wait for 30 days; Venice later made it 40 ( quaranta giorni ), which gives us 'quarantine'.
A world turned upside down

So many workers died that survivors could demand higher wages. In England, laws tried to freeze wages, which angered people. The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 followed, partly from this anger. Some historians say that, in the long run, the Black Death weakened serfdom in Western Europe.
It kept returning

Plague came back in waves for 400 years: London's Great Plague in 1665 and Marseille in 1720. Europe slowly learned about quarantine and isolation. The plague was not a one-time event but a recurring shadow.
Is 'Ring a Ring o' Roses' about the plague?

Myth: the nursery rhyme describes plague symptoms. Fact: there is no evidence for that. The rhyme was first written down in the late 1800s. Folklorists say the plague link was added in the 20th century. Another point: rats were not alone. Some researchers argue that human fleas and lice also helped spread it. That is still being tested.
Meanwhile in India…
Bombay 1896
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Black Death hit Europe in 1347-1351. Yersinia pestis is the confirmed cause. Perhaps a third to a half of Europeans died. Quarantine began in Ragusa and Venice. India's plague came in 1896. Think about it How do societies change after a huge loss of workers? Why do people look for scapegoats in a panic?
The Hundred Years' War: Longbows, Plague and Joan of Arc
A war that lasted 116 years

From 1337 to 1453 England and France fought on and off over the French crown, land and trade. The war is famous for longbows, knights, the Black Death and a teenage girl who led an army. It also helped to shape the idea of England and France as nations, with their own kings, taxes and armies. Many of the battles were small. The war's effects were huge.
A king claims a throne

In 1337 Edward III of England claimed the French crown through his mother, Isabella, sister of the last French king. Philip VI of France was already on the throne, and the French would not accept an English king. Other disputes made things worse. The duchy of Gascony was English land in France, and the wool trade of Flanders tied the economies of the two countries together. Each side wanted control of the other.
The longbow beats the knight

At Crécy in 1346 English archers with longbows shot down French knights and crossbowmen. At Poitiers in 1356 the French king John II was captured. The battles changed how Europeans saw the knight. Henry V's victory at Agincourt in 1415 was even more dramatic. The French army was far larger, but it got stuck in the mud, and thousands of French nobles were killed or captured.
Jean Froissart's chronicle

Jean Froissart (c. 1337–c. 1405) A poet and chronicler from the county of Hainaut, Froissart wrote a huge account of the wars. He loved knightly courage and the grand style of battles. He wrote for rich patrons, so his story favours the nobles. Read him for the feel of the age, and check him against other sources for the facts.
The war in key dates
The war did not run without a break. It was a series of campaigns, truces and sieges across France.
Joan of Arc at Orléans

Joan of Arc was a young peasant woman from Domrémy who said she heard voices of saints. In 1429 she joined the French army and helped lift the English siege of Orléans. Soon after, the Dauphin was crowned as Charles VII at Reims. Joan was captured in 1430. An English-backed court tried her and had her burned at Rouen in 1431. In 1456 a new court declared her trial unjust, and she is now a saint of the Catholic Church.
A war that lasted a hundred years?

The name "Hundred Years' War" suggests one long, unbroken fight. The picture is useful for school lessons, but it is misleading. Historians point out that there were long truces, quiet decades and sudden bursts of fighting. The name came later, and the war was made up of many separate conflicts. Historians argue about the best way to divide them into phases.
The Black Death and the peasants

The Black Death arrived in England in 1348. It killed perhaps a third to a half of the population across Europe, which led to labour shortages and higher wages. Armies struggled to find men. In 1381 English peasants rose in revolt over poll taxes and the harsh rules of serfdom. The rebellion was crushed, but it showed how the war, the plague and taxes were tied together.
The war made states stronger

To pay for the war, kings raised taxes and borrowed money. In France, Charles VII created permanent companies of soldiers in the 1440s, one of the earliest standing armies in Europe. Historians argue that the war helped build modern states. Taxes, professional armies and national feeling grew stronger, though the process took centuries. The English language also gained ground at court and in law.
The end at Castillon

The war effectively ended in 1453 at the battle of Castillon in Gascony. The French artillery, using large cannon, defeated the English army led by John Talbot, who was killed. England kept only Calais. The loss of Gascony ended more than three hundred years of English rule in southwestern France. English kings would still claim the French crown for centuries, but the war was over.
Meanwhile in India…

While England and France fought, the Delhi Sultanate in India was expanding fast. Alauddin Khalji, who ruled from 1296 to 1316, pushed his armies deep into the Deccan and the far south. In 1311 his general Malik Kafur raided the Pandya city of Madurai. Such raids brought loot and tribute to Delhi. They also show a parallel: two great powers on opposite ends of Eurasia were running wars of plunder and state-building in the same century.
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The war ran from 1337 to 1453. Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415) were key English victories. Joan of Arc relieved Orléans in 1429 and was burned in 1431. The Black Death struck in 1348. The war ended at Castillon in 1453, with French artillery. Think about it Did longbows change war more than knights did? Did the war build nations, or did it just drain money?
Mansa Musa and the Empires of West Africa
The pilgrim who crashed Cairo's gold market

In 1324, a king from West Africa arrived in Cairo on the way to Mecca. He came with a huge caravan and so much gold that he gave and spent it freely. An Arab writer, al-Umari, said the price of gold in Cairo stayed low for about twelve years. His name was Mansa Musa .
The Mali Empire

Mali was founded around 1235 by Sundiata Keita , who defeated a rival king at the battle of Kirina . His story is told in the oral epic of the griots. Mali sat on the Niger river, between the forest where gold was mined and the Sahara desert where salt came from.
Gold for salt
Caravans of camels crossed the Sahara. The Mali rulers taxed the trade. Timbuktu and Gao became rich towns.
The Hajj of 1324

Musa ruled from about 1312 to 1337. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 is the stuff of legend. Accounts speak of tens of thousands of people and many camels carrying gold. Numbers are probably exaggerated, but the display clearly shocked Cairo. On the way home he brought back scholars and an architect. In Timbuktu a great mosque, Djinguereber , and later Sankore became centres of learning.
On the map

A Spanish map of 1375, the Catalan Atlas , shows a king on a throne holding a golden nugget, labelled as the ruler of Mali. It put West Africa on Europe's mind. Ibn Battuta, the great traveller, visited Mali in 1352-53, in the reign of Musa's brother Sulayman.
After Mali

Mali weakened in the 1400s. The Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali and then Askia Muhammad took over, with Gao as capital. Timbuktu's libraries kept thousands of manuscripts. Songhai fell to a Moroccan invasion in 1591.
Was Musa the richest man ever?

Myth: he was worth hundreds of billions of dollars. Fact: there are no records to calculate this. Medieval wealth cannot be compared with today's. What we can say: he was famously generous and Mali was extremely rich in gold. Also, Musa did not 'found' Timbuktu; it was already a town. Another caution: our main sources are Arabic writers, who may exaggerate.
Meanwhile in India…
Two travellers' worlds
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Mali was founded by Sundiata around 1235. Gold and salt drove the trade. Musa's Hajj in 1324 became famous. Timbuktu became a scholarly city. Songhai followed Mali. Think about it Why did gold in Cairo 'lose value'? What makes a source reliable when it comes from outsiders?
The Maya, Aztecs and Inca
Three huge civilisations that never knew Rome or China existed
While Europe, Asia and Africa traded, the Americas grew their own cities, calendars and empires. Pyramids in jungles, floating gardens, and a knotted-string accounting system. Let us meet them.
The Maya: maths and glyphs

The classic Maya (about 250-900 CE) built city-states like Tikal and Palenque in today's Mexico, Guatemala and Belize. They tracked stars, used zero in their number system, and had a full writing system of glyphs. It was largely deciphered in the late 20th century, building on work by Yuri Knorozov in the 1950s. Their kings fought wars between cities, and played a ritual ball game.
The Aztecs: city on a lake

The Mexica (Aztecs) founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325. With causeways and farming plots called chinampas , it may have held about 200,000 people. Spaniards said it was bigger than any city they knew.
The Inca: no writing, no problem

The Inca empire, Tawantinsuyu ('four parts together'), ruled from Cusco and stretched about 4,000 km along the Andes. Under Pachacuti , from about 1438, it grew quickly. They had no writing as we know it. They kept records with quipu , knotted strings. They built a huge road network, with relay runners, and terrace farms on steep mountainsides. Machu Picchu was built around 1450.
Why did the Aztecs and Inca fall?

In 1519, Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico with a small force and many native allies who resented Aztec rule. Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Smallpox, new to the Americas, killed huge numbers. In 1532, Francisco Pizarro trapped the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca. The Inca were already weakened by a civil war and by disease.
The Maya never vanished

In the 800s-900s, many southern Maya cities were abandoned. Possible reasons include drought, war and over-farming. Historians still argue about the weight of each. But the Maya themselves did not disappear. Millions of Maya people live in Mexico and Guatemala today and speak Mayan languages.
Did the Maya predict the end of the world in 2012?

Myth: yes. Fact: the Maya Long Count calendar completed a major cycle, a b'ak'tun , on 21 December 2012. That was like a car odometer turning over. Maya texts mention dates thousands of years in the future. There was no doomsday prophecy. Another myth: 'the Aztecs mistook Cortes for a god'. This idea is now seen as post-conquest legend by many historians.
Meanwhile in India…
Zero, chillies and a lost link
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Maya had zero, a calendar and a glyph script. Tenochtitlan was a lake city of about 200,000. The Inca used quipu and roads without writing. Cortes fell on Tenochtitlan in 1521; Pizarro took Atahualpa in 1532. Maya people are still here. Think about it Why do big empires fall quickly when disease strikes? What does zero in both India and Maya say about independent invention?
Polynesian Navigators
They crossed the biggest ocean on Earth with no maps, no compass, and no metal

Look at a map of the Pacific. A triangle with corners at Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island covers about 10 million square km, mostly sea. By around 1300 CE, Polynesians had settled all of it. How? Stars, waves, birds and brilliance.
The long road east

The ancestors came from island Southeast Asia. The Lapita people, known for stamped pottery, spread through Melanesia and then to Tonga and Samoa. After a pause, their descendants pushed east into the huge open ocean.
Reading the sea

Navigators memorised the rising and setting points of stars. They read the shape of ocean swells, the flight of land birds at dawn and dusk, and clouds that stay above islands. A skilled navigator could sense land before seeing it. They sailed double-hulled voyaging canoes with sails, carrying plants, pigs, chickens and families. This was planned settlement, not drifting.
Proving it can be done

Some Western scholars once thought the Polynesians could only have drifted by accident. In 1976 the canoe Hokule'a sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti without instruments, guided by the Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug . It proved intentional voyaging was possible. Piailug, from Satawal, taught Hawaiian sailors their own lost art.
Did they reach South America?

The sweet potato, from South America, was grown across Polynesia before Europeans came. In 2020 a genetic study (Ioannidis et al.) found Native American ancestry in some Polynesian islanders, from contact around 1200 CE. So someone made contact. Who sailed which way is debated.
The last big settlements

New Zealand, Aotearoa, was one of the last large places to be settled, around 1250-1300. The Maori developed their own culture there. Rapa Nui people carved the giant moai statues. The tale that Rapa Nui 'collapsed itself' is debated. Researchers argue about the role of rats, European disease and slave raids.
Kon-Tiki or Asia?

In 1947 the Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl sailed the raft Kon-Tiki from Peru to prove South Americans settled Polynesia. A raft can drift, but language, DNA and archaeology show settlers came from the west . Also, dates of settlement for Hawaii vary a lot by method and the numbers above are best estimates, not certain.
Meanwhile in India…
Monsoon sailors
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Lapita ancestors spread through the Pacific from about 1300 BCE. Navigators used stars, swells and birds. Hokule'a (1976) showed deliberate voyages were possible. DNA suggests contact with South America around 1200 CE. Austronesian sailors also reached Madagascar. Think about it How do you pass a skill down without writing? Why is the 'accidental drift' idea so hard to believe now?
The Renaissance
A bank, a family and a dome that should not have stood

In 1418, Florence announced a contest. The great cathedral had a huge gap in its roof, wider than anyone knew how to cover without wooden scaffolding. A goldsmith named Filippo Brunelleschi said he could do it. He did. The dome was finished in 1436, and Europe's imagination went off like a firework.
Why Florence?

Italian cities like Florence, Venice and Milan had grown rich on trade and banking, even after the Black Death. The Medici family ran Europe's top bank and ruled Florence from 1434 under Cosimo de' Medici. Rich families paid for art to show off. Competition between cities pushed artists to outdo each other.
Looking back to look forward

Scholars like Petrarch (1304-1374) hunted for lost Latin texts and admired ancient Rome. This 'humanism' put human achievement at the centre. After 1453, Greek scholars from Constantinople brought more old books to Italy. The word rinascita (rebirth) was used by the artist-writer Vasari in the 1500s. The word 'Renaissance' was popularised by historian Jacob Burckhardt in 1860.
Three geniuses

Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) painted the Mona Lisa and filled notebooks with machines and anatomy. Michelangelo carved David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-12) from high scaffolding. Raphael painted The School of Athens around 1509-11.
A cold look at power

Niccolo Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, published after his death in 1532. He said a ruler must deal with the world as it is, not as it should be. People called its advice ruthless. Others read it as an honest study of power. He has given us the word 'Machiavellian'.
The Renaissance spreads

Ideas moved north with the printing press. Erasmus of Rotterdam, Thomas More and later Shakespeare drew on Renaissance humanism. Perspective, anatomy and realism changed painting everywhere. Other people were left out: women artists were few, though some, like Sofonisba Anguissola, did get fame.
Was it really a break with the Middle Ages?

Burckhardt saw it as the birth of the modern individual. Many historians now say medieval Europe was not 'dark': universities, cathedrals and science thrived. Renaissance ideas had medieval roots. Also, a common myth says medieval people thought the Earth was flat. Educated people knew it was round, and that includes Columbus's critics.
Meanwhile in India…
Hampi, Fatehpur Sikri and a Jesuit gift
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Florence's wealth and the Medici paid for art. Humanism revived classical learning. Brunelleschi's dome was finished in 1436. Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513. Historians question the neat 'break' with the Middle Ages. Think about it Does art flourish with rich patrons or despite them? Is Machiavelli a cynic or a realist?
The Printing Press and the Reformation
One man's list of complaints went viral in 1517

On 31 October 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther sent 95 arguments against the sale of indulgences to church leaders. Tradition says he nailed them to a church door in Wittenberg. Historians are unsure. Within weeks, printers had copied it across Germany. Without the press, it might have been forgotten.
Gutenberg's machine

Johannes Gutenberg , a goldsmith in Mainz, built a printing press with movable metal type around 1450. The Gutenberg Bible appeared around 1455. About 180 copies were printed, and 49 survive in whole or part. By 1500, Europe had printed perhaps 20 million volumes in presses in over 200 towns. Books became cheaper than manuscripts.
Why indulgences?
An indulgence was a church document that reduced punishment for sins. Luther's attack on its sale was the spark.
Here I stand

At the Diet of Worms (1521), Emperor Charles V ordered Luther to take back his writings. Luther refused. The line 'Here I stand, I can do no other' is attached to him, but many historians think it was added later. A friendly prince, Frederick of Saxony, hid him in Wartburg Castle. There Luther translated the New Testament into German (1522).
Many Reformations

Other reformers emerged. Zwingli in Zurich, and John Calvin in Geneva, whose ideas shaped Presbyterian and Reformed churches. In England, Henry VIII broke from Rome in 1534 (the Act of Supremacy) mostly because he wanted an heir and a new marriage. The Catholic Church answered with the Counter-Reformation and the Jesuits (founded 1540).
Wars of religion

Fighting broke out. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each German prince choose Catholic or Lutheran for his lands. Later came the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648), which killed millions, especially in Germany. It ended with the Peace of Westphalia, often linked to the idea of sovereign states.
Did Gutenberg invent printing?

Myth: yes. Fact: China had woodblock printing by the 8th century and movable type by about 1040. Korea printed a Buddhist book with metal type, the Jikji , in 1377. Gutenberg's real contribution was a practical system for Europe: an adjustable mould, a press, and oil-based ink. Also, Luther did not intend to split the Church at first.

Five things to remember Gutenberg's press (c. 1450) cut the cost of books. Luther's 95 Theses (1517) spread by print. Protestant movements and the Counter-Reformation split Europe. The Thirty Years' War ended in 1648. India's first printing came in Goa, 1556. Think about it What would Luther have achieved without print? What is today's printing press?
The Ottomans: Masters of Three Continents
A tiny frontier band that ended up running Cairo, Baghdad and Budapest

Around 1300, a Turkish chief named Osman led a small band in north-west Anatolia. Six hundred years later, his family still ruled, in a state that straddled Europe, Asia and Africa. The Ottoman story is one of the longest in history.
The rise

In 1453, 21-year-old Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, the Byzantine capital, and made it his own (Istanbul). In 1517 Selim I beat the Mamluks and took Egypt, Syria and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
Suleiman the Magnificent

Suleiman I ruled 1520-1566. He won at Mohacs (1526) and besieged Vienna (1529) but did not take it. His navy ruled much of the Mediterranean. Turks call him Kanuni, 'the Lawgiver'. His wife Hurrem Sultan (Roxelana), a former slave, became very powerful. The architect Sinan built the Suleymaniye Mosque (1550-57).
Soldiers taken as boys

Under the devshirme system, Christian boys from the Balkans were taken, converted and trained as officials and elite soldiers, the Janissaries . Some rose to be grand viziers. It was brutal for families, yet it let talented outsiders rise. Over time Janissaries became powerful and political. Sultan Mahmud II destroyed them in 1826.
How it governed

The Ottomans let religious communities, the millets , manage their own affairs (the system developed over time). Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 found refuge there. Trade, coffee and coffeehouses boomed. Yet early sultans practised fratricide: Mehmed II declared it acceptable for a new sultan to kill his brothers. Later princes were confined instead.
Decline, or change?

From the 1700s, Europe's armies and economies pulled ahead. In the 1800s the empire became 'the sick man of Europe' as it lost lands. It joined World War I on Germany's side and lost. In 1922 the sultanate was abolished, and in 1924 the caliphate.
Did the Ottomans decline?

The old view said the empire decayed after Suleiman. Newer historians say it adapted, reformed and survived 350 more years. The Tanzimat reforms (1839-76) tried to modernise. Also, the Armenian genocide (1915-16) remains a heated issue. Many scholars and countries call it genocide; Turkey rejects that label.

Zheng He's Treasure Fleets
China sent the biggest fleet in the world, then stopped

In 1405, a fleet of hundreds of ships, carrying nearly 28,000 men, left Nanjing for the Indian Ocean. It was commanded by a eunuch admiral from a Muslim family in Yunnan. Sixty years before Columbus and Vasco da Gama, China ruled the waves. Then it went home.
The admiral

Zheng He was born Ma He in 1371 in Yunnan. As a boy he was captured by Ming forces, made a eunuch and served the prince who became the Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402-1424). Yongle wanted to show China's glory, win tribute from foreign rulers, and perhaps look for his rival, the vanished previous emperor.
Seven voyages

The fleets visited Vietnam, Java, Sumatra, Sri Lanka, India, Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast, perhaps reaching Mecca by some members. The treasure ships were huge, though old claims of about 120 metres long are debated; many scholars think they were smaller.
A giraffe for the emperor

In 1414 a ruler from Bengal sent a giraffe to China (some say it was brought later from Africa). Courtiers called it a qilin , a lucky mythical beast, and celebrated. The fleet also took silk and porcelain, and returned with spices, gems and ambassadors.
Why did it stop?

After Yongle died, Confucian officials thought the voyages too costly. Money was needed to fight the Mongols and to rebuild the capital at Beijing. The new emperor Xuande ended the voyages after 1433. A story says officials burned the records. Historians now doubt it; the documents may simply have been lost or ignored.
Compare with Europe
China sailed for prestige, with a vast navy. Europeans sailed for profit and kept coming.
Did Zheng He discover America?

Myth: the 2002 book 1421: The Year China Discovered the World by Gavin Menzies claimed the Chinese reached America, and more. Fact: historians reject it. No Chinese records, no archaeology and no maps support it. It sold well but is considered fantasy. What is true: his fleet really was spectacular, and it was real naval power.

Five things to remember Zheng He led seven voyages (1405-1433). He served the Yongle emperor. The fleets were huge for their time. Costs and politics ended the voyages. Calicut was a key stop; da Gama came 65 years later. Think about it Is power measured by what you can do, or what you choose to do? Why did Europeans keep going where China stopped?
Columbus, Conquest and the Columbian Exchange
The man who sailed to 'India' and never realised where he was

On 12 October 1492, after about ten weeks at sea, a lookout on the Pinta shouted 'Land!' Christopher Columbus stepped ashore on an island in the Bahamas. He was sure he had reached the edge of Asia. He died in 1506, still believing it.
Why sail west?

Since the Ottomans controlled eastern routes, Europeans wanted a sea route to Asia's spices and silk. Portugal was sailing around Africa. Columbus, from Genoa, proposed going west instead. He got ships from Spain's queen Isabella and king Ferdinand: the Santa Maria, Pinta and Nina . He had guessed Earth was smaller than it is. Educated people knew it was round, but his critics rightly said the distance was far bigger.
The map is redrawn

Spain and Portugal agreed in the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) to split the new lands between them. A German map of 1507 first used the name America , after Amerigo Vespucci, who argued it was a new continent. In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India round Africa. Two routes, one world.
The Columbian Exchange
The historian Alfred Crosby named this the Columbian Exchange in 1972. Potatoes helped Europe's population grow. Horses changed Plains life. But germs were deadly.
Disease, gold and silver

The Taino people of the Caribbean were nearly wiped out within decades by disease, forced labour and violence. In the mainland, smallpox killed vast numbers. Estimates of the pre-1492 population and the fall vary widely; many scholars say the Americas lost the majority of their people in the first century or so. Spanish mines like Potosi (Bolivia) poured silver into the world economy.
Columbus himself

Columbus was a brave sailor and a harsh governor. Spanish officials arrested him in 1500 over his rule in Hispaniola. Today many places debate statues and holidays named for him. The debate is about the person, but also about what 1492 started. Both points are true: the voyage changed history, and it began a catastrophe for many.
Did Columbus prove the Earth was round?

Myth: everyone thought it was flat until Columbus. Fact: educated Europeans had known it was round since Greek times. Eratosthenes (about 240 BCE) even estimated its size. Columbus was wrong about the size, and if the Americas had not been there, his ships would likely have run out of food. Another correction: Norse sailors reached North America around 500 years earlier.

The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals and diseases. Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Think about it Can a voyage be both great and terrible? What would Europe eat without the Americas?
The Atlantic Slave Trade
The biggest forced migration in history

Between about 1500 and 1866, roughly 12.5 million Africans were put on ships bound for the Americas. About 10.7 million survived the voyage. That figure comes from the Slave Voyages database, built from ship records. This is a hard story. But it is a central one. Much of the modern world was built on it.
How it began

In the 1440s, Portuguese sailors began taking captives from West Africa. After Europeans began growing sugar in Brazil and the Caribbean, they needed huge numbers of workers. Native American populations had been devastated by disease. Sugar, then tobacco, coffee and cotton, depended on enslaved labour.
The trade loop

The 'triangular trade' is a simple picture. Real routes were many, and Brazil alone received nearly half of all captives. Britain, Portugal, France, Spain, the Netherlands and later the US were all involved.
The Middle Passage

Captives were chained below decks in crowded, unhealthy spaces. Roughly one in seven died at sea. Revolts took place on ships. In 1789 Olaudah Equiano , a formerly enslaved man living in Britain, published his autobiography. It was a bestseller and helped the abolition movement.
Africans and the trade

African rulers and merchants also took part: kingdoms such as Dahomey and Asante sold captives, often from wars. Historians argue how much their choices were free and how much European demand and guns forced events. The effects on African societies were deep and long-lasting: population loss, fear and war.
Abolition
Britain paid huge compensation to slave owners in 1833, not to the enslaved. The Royal Navy patrolled West Africa to stop ships, with limited success.
How much did slavery build Western wealth?

Eric Williams argued in Capitalism and Slavery (1944) that profits from slavery fed Britain's industrial revolution, and that abolition came partly for economic reasons. Many historians have challenged parts of his argument; the debate continues. One fact is not debated: enslaved people did not simply accept it. Revolts, escapes and communities of the escaped (like Palmares in Brazil) were widespread.

The Scientific Revolution
A telescope, an apple story and a very angry Church

In 1609-10, an Italian professor named Galileo pointed a telescope at the sky and saw four moons circling Jupiter. They did not circle Earth. That was a problem for everyone who thought everything did. This was the beginning of seeing the world with evidence first.
Moving the Earth
Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres in 1543, placing the Sun at the centre. The same year Vesalius published a book on human anatomy based on dissection.
Kepler and Galileo

Johannes Kepler used data from Tycho Brahe to show planets move in ellipses , not perfect circles (1609). Galileo backed Copernicus with telescope sights: Jupiter's moons, Venus's phases, craters on the Moon. In 1633 the Inquisition forced Galileo to recant. He lived the rest of his life under house arrest.
Newton ties it together

Isaac Newton published the Principia in 1687. His laws of motion and universal gravitation explained both a falling apple and the orbit of the Moon with the same rules. That idea, that nature follows mathematical laws that humans can find, changed how people thought.
A new way of finding things out

Francis Bacon urged people to learn by experiment and observation. Descartes said to doubt everything and build up through reason. The Royal Society (1660) and the French Academy (1666) spread findings in journals. Instruments such as the microscope and the barometer opened new worlds.
Not a single 'revolution'

Many of the scientists were deeply religious. Newton wrote more on alchemy and theology than on physics. Ideas moved slowly, and plenty of old beliefs lasted. Historians even debate whether to call it a 'revolution'. Some prefer 'a long series of changes'.
Did an apple hit Newton's head?

Myth: yes, and he shouted 'Eureka'. Fact: Newton himself later told friends that seeing an apple fall set him thinking about gravity. The head-bonk is a later embellishment. Another myth: Galileo was tortured or jailed in a dungeon. He wasn't. And 'Yet it moves' is probably a legend.

The Enlightenment
Dare to think for yourself

In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered a magazine's question, 'What is Enlightenment?' His answer: it is humans leaving behind their self-imposed laziness in thinking. His motto was Sapere aude , 'Dare to know'. That daring changed kings, churches and the way we vote.
Reason in the cafes

The Enlightenment (roughly the late 1600s to the late 1700s) grew out of the Scientific Revolution. If reason can explain the planets, why not government, religion and trade? Ideas travelled in coffeehouses, salons hosted by clever women in Paris, and print. The huge Encyclopedie of Diderot (1751-72) tried to gather all knowledge.
Four big voices

John Locke ( Two Treatises , 1689): people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and can remove a ruler who breaks the trust. Montesquieu ( The Spirit of the Laws , 1748): separate the powers of government.
The pen is mightier

Voltaire fought for tolerance and attacked religious persecution, after the Calas affair (1762), in which an innocent Protestant was executed. Rousseau ( The Social Contract , 1762) wrote that man is born free but is everywhere in chains, and argued rule should follow the 'general will'. Rousseau and Voltaire disliked each other intensely.
Money and women

Adam Smith , in The Wealth of Nations (1776), argued free markets create wealth. Mary Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) and said women need education to be equal. Most Enlightenment writers did not extend 'all men' to women.
Kings who liked ideas

Some rulers, called 'enlightened despots', used reason to reform without sharing power: Frederick the Great of Prussia, Catherine the Great of Russia, Joseph II of Austria. Ideas also lit the revolutions in America and France.
Did Voltaire say 'I disapprove of what you say...'?

Myth: Voltaire said, 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.' Fact: that line was written in 1906 by Evelyn Beatrice Hall, summing up his attitude. He never wrote it. Also, many Enlightenment thinkers held racist views or profited from slavery. Historians argue whether those ideas were part of the Enlightenment or a betrayal of it.

The American Revolution
The Tea Party was about monopoly, not the price of tea

On 16 December 1773, men dressed as Mohawks boarded three ships in Boston harbour and dumped 342 chests of tea into the water. It looks like a story about a tax. It was really about a company. The company was the East India Company, and it ties directly to us.
Taxes and a lost war

Britain won the Seven Years' War (1756-63) but was deep in debt. It taxed the American colonies: the Stamp Act (1765), then duties on tea, glass and paper. Colonists said they had no representatives in Parliament, so taxes were unfair: 'no taxation without representation'. The Boston Massacre (1770) left five colonists dead.
Tea and trouble

The Tea Act (1773) actually made East India Company tea cheaper, even with the tax, but gave the Company a monopoly and accepted Parliament's right to tax. Merchants and radicals objected. Britain answered with harsh 'Coercive Acts' in 1774. Fighting began in April 1775 at Lexington and Concord.
Declaring independence

Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration , adopted on 4 July 1776 (the vote for independence was on 2 July). It said all men are created equal and have the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Jefferson himself held enslaved people.
How they won

George Washington's Continental Army was often short of food and money. The big turn came when the Americans won at Saratoga in 1777, which convinced France to join them in 1778. In 1781 a French fleet and army helped trap General Cornwallis at Yorktown . Britain recognised independence in the Treaty of Paris (1783).
Making a country

The first system, the Articles of Confederation, was weak. A convention at Philadelphia wrote the Constitution in 1787, with separation of powers, a President and a Congress. The Bill of Rights followed (1791). The revolution was a model for others, but it left slavery alone and gave voting rights to few.
Was it a real revolution?

Some say it was a political break, not a social upheaval, since the same rich men kept power. Others say the radical ideas of equality and republican government changed the world. Myth check: 'Tea tax went up.' It did not; the price of legal tea was falling. The argument was about principle and about the Company's power.

The French Revolution
A prison with seven prisoners became the symbol of a revolution

On 14 July 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a fortress prison. They wanted gunpowder. Inside, there were only seven prisoners. But the Bastille stood for royal power, and its fall shook Europe.
Bankrupt kingdom

France was broke after wars (including helping America). Society had three Estates : clergy, nobles, and everyone else. The Third Estate paid most taxes and had the least say. Bad harvests made bread dear. In May 1789 Louis XVI called the Estates-General to raise money. The Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath (20 June).
Rights and a march

The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August 1789) said men are born free and equal. In October, thousands of Parisian women marched to Versailles and brought the royal family to Paris.
The Terror

In 1793 France was at war with most of Europe and torn by civil war. The Committee of Public Safety, with Robespierre , ruled by fear. The guillotine was used on thousands. Around 17,000 were officially executed; many more died in prisons and revolts, with some estimates of 40,000 deaths. In July 1794 Robespierre himself was guillotined.
Slogans and changes

The revolutionaries abolished feudal privileges, made a new calendar and metric measures, and confiscated Church lands. 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' became the motto. Women did not win the vote. Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791 and was guillotined in 1793.
After the storm

The chaos ended with a young general taking power in 1799: Napoleon. Historians still argue whether the Revolution brought freedom or just a new strongman. But after 1789, kings everywhere had to worry about what their people might do.
'Let them eat cake'

Myth: Marie Antoinette said it when told that the poor had no bread. Fact: no evidence she said it. A similar line appears in Rousseau's Confessions , written when she was a child, about 'a great princess'. It is propaganda. Also, the Bastille's taking was not about freeing prisoners, and the Revolution did not end the monarchy overnight; it happened over three years.

Napoleon
The man who crowned himself

On 2 December 1804, in Notre-Dame cathedral, the Pope waited to crown the new emperor of the French. Napoleon took the crown from the Pope's hands and put it on his own head. It was a message: I owe nobody.
The islander

Napoleon Bonaparte was born in 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, just after France bought the island. He became an artillery officer. He won fame at Toulon (1793), then in Italy (1796-97). In 1798 he invaded Egypt, partly to threaten British routes to India. He won on land but his fleet was destroyed by Nelson at the Nile. In 1799, he returned and took power in a coup.
Law and glory

As First Consul and then Emperor, Napoleon made the Napoleonic Code (1804): equal rights before the law, protection of property, and religious toleration, but fewer rights for women. It shaped many countries' laws. He won huge victories, like Austerlitz (2 December 1805). Yet Nelson's win at Trafalgar (October 1805) kept Britain safe at sea. He sold Louisiana to the US in 1803.
The rise and fall
In 1812 he invaded Russia with about half a million men. Disease, hunger and the Russian winter destroyed the army; only a small fraction came back. In 1814 he was forced to abdicate.
Hundred Days

He escaped from Elba in 1815 and regained France. At Waterloo (18 June 1815), British and Prussian forces under Wellington and Blucher beat him. He was exiled to St Helena, a lonely island in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.
Legacy

He spread ideas of the Revolution across Europe, breaking old states and awakening nationalism. His wars also killed millions. Afterwards the Congress of Vienna (1814-15) tried to restore the old order and balance of power.
Was Napoleon short?

Myth: he was tiny. Fact: he was about 5 feet 6 or 7 inches in modern measure, average or slightly above for his time. French inches were longer than English ones, and British cartoons drew him as small. His nickname 'le petit caporal' was affectionate. Another point: 'Napoleon complex' is a myth built on that error.

The Haitian Revolution
The only successful slave revolt that created a country

In the 1780s, the French colony of Saint-Domingue produced more sugar and coffee than any other place on Earth. It was also a hell for about half a million enslaved people. In 1791, they rose. Thirteen years later, they had defeated the armies of France, Spain and Britain, and founded a nation: Haiti.
The richest colony

Saint-Domingue had about 500,000 enslaved people, perhaps 30,000 free people of colour and a similar number of whites. Death rates were so high that planters constantly bought more captives. When the French Revolution began in 1789, the colony fought over who was covered by 'Rights of Man'.
August 1791

In August 1791 a huge uprising began in the north, said to have been launched after a ceremony at Bois Caiman (details are debated). Plantations burned. Leaders emerged, among them Toussaint Louverture , a formerly enslaved man in his late forties who had learned to read.
A leader and a betrayal

In 1794, France's revolutionary government abolished slavery, and Toussaint joined the French side. He ruled the island as governor. Napoleon wanted slavery back. In 1802 he sent a big army. Toussaint was seized by trickery and died in a French prison in April 1803.
Victory

Disease, especially yellow fever, killed many French soldiers. Under Jean-Jacques Dessalines , the rebels won the battle of Vertieres (November 1803). On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared independence, the first Black republic and the first free state in Latin America. The name Haiti was a native Taino word.
The price of freedom

France, and other countries, refused to recognise Haiti. In 1825, France demanded 150 million francs as 'compensation' for lost property, later reduced to 90 million. Haiti borrowed from French banks and paid until 1947. Historians link this debt to Haiti's long poverty. The US only recognised Haiti in 1862.
Is Haiti poor because it is 'cursed'?

Myth: Haiti's troubles come from a curse or a pact. Fact: historians point to concrete causes: the indemnity, trade embargoes, destroyed plantations, later foreign interference and political instability. Another effect: Napoleon lost Saint-Domingue and soon sold Louisiana to the US in 1803. The revolution also terrified slave-owners across the Americas and inspired enslaved people elsewhere.

The Industrial Revolution
Why did a rainy island change how the whole world works?

Around 1760, one small country began making things with machines and coal instead of hands and muscle. Within a century, the world had factories, railways and slums. That island was Britain. The question is why.
Coal, cotton and steam

Thomas Newcomen built an early steam engine in 1712. James Watt greatly improved it from the 1760s-70s. Spinning machines such as Hargreaves's jenny and Arkwright's water frame (1760s) multiplied output.
Rail and the city

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830, with Stephenson's engines. Manchester grew from a town into a vast 'cotton city'. Factories ran on fixed hours. Time itself got stricter. Trade in raw cotton relied on slave plantations in the American South.
The human price

Workers, including young children, laboured 12-14 hours in noisy mills. Cities lacked clean water and drains, and cholera and typhus spread. Slow reforms followed, such as the Factory Act of 1833, which limited children's hours. In the long run, living standards rose, but for several decades many people were worse off.
Why Britain?

Historians argue. Ideas: coal near the surface, high wages that made machines worth building, an overseas empire for markets and raw materials, secure property rights and a culture of tinkering. Kenneth Pomeranz ( The Great Divergence , 2000) stressed coal and colonies. No single cause is accepted by all.
Were the Luddites against technology?

Myth: Luddites (1811-16) smashed machines because they hated progress. Fact: they were skilled textile workers protesting low pay and loss of their trade. Machine-breaking was a way to bargain. The government sent more troops against them than it had sent to fight Napoleon in some years; the law made machine-breaking punishable by death in 1812.

Japan's Meiji Leap
Four black ships, and a country changed in 15 years

In July 1853, American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay. They were steam-powered and painted black. Japan, closed to most outsiders for over 200 years, now had to decide. It chose to change faster than any big country had.
The shock
The Tokugawa shogunate looked weak. Young samurai from Satsuma and Choshu rebelled. In 1868 they 'restored' the young Emperor Meiji (aged 15) to power.
Remaking a state

The new government abolished the old feudal domains (1871), ended samurai privileges, created a conscript army (1873), built railways (first line 1872), set up schools and factories. The Iwakura Mission (1871-73) toured the US and Europe to learn. A Constitution came in 1889, with an elected Diet but strong powers for the emperor.
The last samurai
Many samurai lost their income. In 1877 Saigo Takamori , once a hero of the Restoration, led the Satsuma Rebellion. Modern conscript soldiers crushed it. It made clear that the old order was gone.
Joining the imperial club

Japan beat China in the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) and took Taiwan. In 1902 it allied with Britain. In 1904-05 it defeated Russia, the first time an Asian power beat a European great power in a modern war. Japan then annexed Korea (1910), becoming an imperial power itself.
Did Japan modernise from nothing?

Myth: a backward country suddenly woke up. Fact: Edo Japan already had big cities (Edo was among the largest in the world), high literacy for the time, banking and trade. Meiji leaders built on that. Also, 'Restoration' was partly a slogan; the real power was held by a small group of ex-samurai officials.
