The Scramble for Africa
In 1870 about a tenth of Africa was ruled by Europeans. By 1914, almost all of it

Imagine losing control of your continent in about 40 years. That is what happened in Africa. Only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent. How? Guns, medicine, railways and a very unusual conference where no African was invited.
The tools
Quinine fought malaria. Steamships went up rivers. The rapid-fire Maxim gun (1884) gave Europeans a huge advantage in battle.
Berlin 1884-85

German chancellor Bismarck hosted a conference in Berlin (November 1884-February 1885). Fourteen states attended, none African. They agreed that to claim land, a power needed 'effective occupation'. It did not draw Africa's map by itself; the carve-up was already under way. But it sparked a rush.
A king's private colony

King Leopold II of Belgium got recognition of the 'Congo Free State' in 1885 as nearly his personal property. Forced rubber collection brought mutilation and killing. Millions died; estimates vary and are debated, with figures like 10 million often cited. After campaigns by E. D. Morel and others, Belgium took it over in 1908.
Resistance

Africans resisted all over. At Adwa on 1 March 1896, Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia crushed an Italian army. The Boer War (1899-1902) pitted Britain against Dutch settlers. In German South West Africa, the Herero and Nama genocide (1904-08) killed tens of thousands. Borders were often straight lines that split peoples and joined rivals. Many modern African conflicts have roots there.
Did Berlin 'divide Africa' in one meeting?

Myth: European leaders sat in Berlin and cut up a map. Fact: the conference dealt with the Congo and the rules for claiming land. Most borders were set later through treaties between powers, and many by field agents. Still, no African ruler had a say, and that is the heart of the injustice.
Meanwhile in India…
Indians in Africa
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember By 1914 Europe controlled almost all Africa. The Berlin Conference (1884-85) set the rules, with no Africans present. Leopold's Congo was among the worst. Ethiopia won at Adwa (1896). Indians built the Uganda Railway. Think about it Why did Europe rush in at that moment? What does Adwa teach?
The Opium Wars and China's Century of Humiliation
A war fought over a drug the British grew in India

In 1839, a Chinese official named Lin Zexu seized over 1,000 tonnes of opium from foreign merchants in Canton and destroyed it in trenches with lime and salt water. That act launched a war, and a century of pain China still remembers.
Tea, silver and opium
The East India Company ran an opium monopoly in India and sold the drug at auction in Calcutta to private traders, who shipped it to China.
First Opium War, 1839-42

Britain sent steam-powered warships and sepoys. China's old forts and ships were no match. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave Britain Hong Kong, five treaty ports and a large payment, and a later treaty gave extra rights to foreigners. It was the first of the 'unequal treaties'.
Second war and a burned palace

In the Second Opium War (1856-60) Britain and France attacked again. In 1860 they looted and burned the Summer Palace in Beijing. Opium trade was legalised. Meanwhile, the Taiping Rebellion (1850-64) tore China apart from inside. Estimates say over 20 million died.
A 'century of humiliation'

Chinese tradition counts about 1839-1949: lost wars, foreign concessions, and the loss of Taiwan to Japan (1895). Many Chinese leaders today use this story to explain their desire for a strong state. Hong Kong stayed British until 1 July 1997.
Was China just backward and closed?

Myth: China refused to trade, so Britain had to force it open. Fact: China traded widely, through Canton under rules the Qing set. The dispute was over a drug that the government had banned, which merchants smuggled. Historians still argue how much opium harmed China's economy, but the war itself began over this trade.
Meanwhile in India…
Poppy fields and Bombay fortunes
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Opium paid for British tea. Lin Zexu destroyed opium in 1839. The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) gave Hong Kong. The Summer Palace was burned in 1860. India's opium revenue fed the empire. Think about it Is a trade that harms a country ever 'free'? How does a past humiliation shape policy today?
The First World War
A wrong turn in Sarajevo lit a fuse across the world

On 28 June 1914, the Austrian heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, was driving through Sarajevo. His car stalled after an earlier bomb attempt failed. A 19-year-old named Gavrilo Princip was standing nearby. He shot the Archduke and his wife. Within six weeks, Europe was at war.
The fuse
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia. Alliances pulled in Russia, Germany, France and Britain. Germany's plan was to knock out France fast. It failed, and the armies dug in.
The trenches

From late 1914 the Western Front was a line of trenches from the sea to Switzerland. Machine guns made charging deadly. On 1 July 1916, the first day of the Somme, Britain suffered about 57,000 casualties, with about 19,000 killed. New horrors: poison gas (used at Ypres in 1915), tanks (1916), aircraft and submarines.
A truce and a long war

At Christmas 1914, soldiers on parts of the front stopped firing and swapped gifts. It was short-lived and not general. In 1917 the US joined after German submarine attacks, while Russia, torn by revolution, left the war. Germany asked for an armistice, which began on 11 November 1918 .
The cost

Roughly 9-10 million soldiers died, plus millions of civilians. Four empires fell: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman. The Treaty of Versailles (1919) blamed Germany and imposed reparations. The 1918-19 influenza pandemic, helped by troop movements, killed many more.
Whose fault was it?

After the war, Germany was blamed. In 1961 Fritz Fischer argued Germany pushed for war. In 2012 Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers argued all powers stumbled into it. A famous myth: soldiers were 'lions led by donkeys'. Historians now say that image is too simple, since commanders learned and tactics improved.
Meanwhile in India…
The forgotten army
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The war began after Sarajevo in 1914. Trench warfare killed millions. Ended on 11 November 1918. Four empires collapsed. Indians served in large numbers. Think about it Why did alliances make a local crisis global? What did India get for its sacrifice?
The Russian Revolution
A sealed train, a tsar's abdication and a revolution in a week

In April 1917, a train carrying Lenin from exile in Switzerland rolled across Germany toward Russia. Germany let it pass, hoping he would weaken Russia's war effort. It worked, beyond what anyone expected.
The tsar falls

Russia in 1917 was exhausted by war, with food shortages. In Petrograd, strikes and women's marches on 8 March (23 February in the old calendar) grew into revolt. Soldiers joined the crowds. Nicholas II abdicated. The Romanov dynasty, 300 years old, was over. A Provisional Government took charge, but kept fighting the war.
Peace, land, bread
Lenin's Bolsheviks promised 'Peace, land and bread'. On 25 October (7 November, new calendar), they took over the capital and government buildings with little fighting.
Civil war

Reds (Bolsheviks) fought Whites (various opponents), with foreign intervention. The war lasted to 1922. Millions died from fighting, famine and disease. The Bolsheviks created the secret police, the Cheka. The tsar and his family were shot in July 1918 at Yekaterinburg.
A new state

In 1922 the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was founded. After Lenin died in 1924, Stalin beat Trotsky in the struggle for power. The state took over industry and farms and ruled by terror in the 1930s. The Revolution inspired communists and anticolonial movements across the world.
Did the Bolsheviks storm the Winter Palace in a huge battle?

Myth: thousands charged the Palace in a bloody fight. Fact: the real seizure was fairly quiet, with few casualties. The famous images come from Eisenstein's 1928 film October and later propaganda. Also: the date. Russia used the Julian calendar until 1918, so the 'October' revolution is on 7 November in our calendar.
Meanwhile in India…
Red ideas travel
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The tsar fell in February 1917. The Bolsheviks took power in October 1917. A civil war lasted to 1922. The USSR was created in 1922. India's thinkers were inspired. Think about it Why did the Provisional Government fail? Is a revolution made by leaders, or by crowds?
The Great Depression
The crash did not cause it alone, but it lit the match

On Tuesday 29 October 1929, panicked investors dumped 16 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Prices crashed. Within four years, a quarter of American workers had no job, and the whole world was in trouble.
Boom to bust
Thousands of US banks failed in the early 1930s, and there was no deposit insurance. World trade shrank by about two thirds.
Wrong medicine

Governments cut spending and raised tariffs. The US Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) set high import taxes, and other countries retaliated. Staying on the gold standard forced many countries into deflation. By 1933 US unemployment was about 25 percent, and in Germany about 6 million were jobless.
The New Deal and Keynes

In 1933 Franklin D. Roosevelt took office and began the New Deal : bank rescue, public works, Social Security (1935). John Maynard Keynes's General Theory (1936) argued that governments should spend to revive demand in a slump. Historians still argue how much the New Deal did; the real recovery came with war spending.
Politics turns ugly

Hardship fed anger. In Germany the Nazis rose from a small party to the largest in 1932. In Japan, the military gained power. The Depression did not make World War II certain, but it made it much likelier.
Did stockbrokers jump from windows?

Myth: after the crash, ruined brokers leapt from skyscrapers by the dozen. Fact: it makes a dramatic story, but records show very few suicides in those weeks. Also, the crash itself did not cause the Depression: weak banks, debt and bad policy turned a crash into a catastrophe.
Meanwhile in India…
Farmers and gold
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The 1929 crash began the slump. Bank failures and falling trade made it a global depression. Wrong policies worsened it. The New Deal and Keynes changed economic thinking. Hardship helped extremists rise. Think about it Should governments spend more in a slump? Why did the Depression hit farmers in India?
Fascism and Nazism
How a dictator was handed power by people who thought they could control him

On 30 January 1933, the German president Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler as chancellor. Conservative politicians thought they could use him and keep him in check. Within 18 months he had no checks left.
Mussolini goes first

Fascism began in Italy. Mussolini , once a socialist, led his Blackshirts in the 'March on Rome' (October 1922). The king asked him to form a government. By 1925 he had made himself dictator. Fascists glorified the nation, the leader and violence, and hated democracy, liberals and socialists.
Hitler's rise

After a failed coup in 1923, Hitler turned to elections. The Nazis won 37 percent in July 1932, their best free result. After the Reichstag fire (February 1933) and the Enabling Act (March 1933), Germany became a one-party dictatorship.
Racism as state policy

The Nazis claimed 'Aryans' were a master race. They stripped Jews of citizenship and rights with the Nuremberg Laws (1935). On 9-10 November 1938 came Kristallnacht , when synagogues and Jewish shops were smashed and about 30,000 Jewish men arrested. Hitler's regime also persecuted Roma, disabled people, homosexuals and political opponents.
Why did it work?

Reasons historians give: economic misery, anger over Versailles, fear of communism, weak democratic habits, clever propaganda by Joseph Goebbels, and violence by the SA. The Nazi state also gave many Germans jobs and national pride. But the same state was a machine of terror, with the Gestapo, camps and no free press.
Was Hitler elected dictator?

Myth: Germans voted him in as dictator. Fact: the Nazis never won a majority in a free election. In November 1932 their share fell to about 33 percent. Hindenburg and conservative politicians appointed Hitler chancellor. He then used emergency powers to destroy democracy. It shows how fragile democracy can be when elites bargain with extremists.
Meanwhile in India…
Bose, Gandhi and Nehru
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Mussolini took power in 1922. Hitler was appointed in January 1933. The Enabling Act ended democracy. Nuremberg Laws and Kristallnacht targeted Jews. Bose, Gandhi and Nehru reacted differently. Think about it How can democracies protect themselves? Why did people support or tolerate the regime?
The Second World War
The deadliest war in history, in five dates

On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Britain and France declared war two days later. Over six years, the war killed an estimated 70-85 million people, most of them civilians. Here is the story in the fewest possible steps.
Blitzkrieg and Britain alone
Germany's fast attack, Blitzkrieg , conquered Poland and then France in six weeks (1940). Britain held out in the Battle of Britain, with Churchill's leadership.
The East and the Pacific

In June 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union. On 7 December 1941 Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and the US entered the war. The Soviets beat Germany at Stalingrad (1942-43). The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people. In June 1944 Allied forces landed in Normandy ( D-Day , 6 June). Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945.
The bomb

The US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August). Japan announced surrender on 15 August; the formal signing was on 2 September. Historians still argue about whether the bombs were needed, or whether the Soviet entry into the war was decisive.
The cost and the aftermath

Cities lay in ruins, and tens of millions were displaced. The war gave birth to the United Nations (1945), the Nuremberg trials, and a world with two superpowers, the US and USSR. It also made colonial empires harder to hold.
Did the war start only in Europe in 1939?

Myth: WWII started with Poland. Fact: in Asia, Japan invaded China in 1937 (or Manchuria in 1931), so for China the war began earlier. Also, Allied victory was not only the work of the US and Britain: the Soviet Union and China bore enormous losses.
Meanwhile in India…
An army, a famine and a movement
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember WWII began in 1939 (earlier in Asia). Germany attacked the USSR in 1941; Pearl Harbor drew in the US. D-Day 1944; Germany surrendered May 1945. Atomic bombs preceded Japan's surrender in August 1945. India contributed troops and suffered a famine. Think about it Was the bombing of cities justified? How did the war speed up decolonisation?
The Holocaust
The murder of six million, planned like paperwork

This lesson is heavy. We tell it plainly because it must be remembered precisely. Between 1933 and 1945, Nazi Germany and its collaborators persecuted Jews and then murdered about six million of them, two thirds of Europe's Jewish population.
Step by step
The process began with exclusion, then ghettos, then killing. After the invasion of the USSR in 1941, mobile units called Einsatzgruppen shot over a million Jews, mostly in pits.
The 'Final Solution'

At the Wannsee Conference (20 January 1942), officials coordinated the plan to murder all European Jews. Death camps such as Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec and Auschwitz-Birkenau used gas chambers. About 1.1 million people were murdered at Auschwitz, around 1 million of them Jews. It needed trains, clerks, police and the silence of many.
Others, and resistance

The Nazis also murdered Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and political prisoners. Jews resisted too, in ghetto uprisings: the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising (April-May 1943) was the largest. Some non-Jews risked their lives to hide Jews. Israel's Yad Vashem honours them as 'Righteous Among the Nations'.
Justice and memory

After the war, the Nuremberg trials (1945-46) tried leading Nazis. Raphael Lemkin, a Polish-Jewish lawyer, coined the word genocide in 1944. The UN adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948. Holocaust Remembrance Day is observed on 27 January, the day Auschwitz was liberated in 1945.
'The Germans didn't know' and 'Jews didn't fight back'

Myth 1: ordinary Germans did not know. Fact: many people saw deportations and knew of killings; how much they knew of the camps is debated, but the persecution was public. Myth 2: Jews went passively. Fact: there was armed resistance in many ghettos and camps, as well as vast spiritual and hidden resistance.
Meanwhile in India…
The Good Maharaja
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember About six million Jews were murdered. The process moved from exclusion to killing. Wannsee coordinated it in January 1942. Others were murdered too; resistance existed. Genocide became a legal term. Think about it Why must we remember specifics? What allows ordinary people to take part in atrocities?
The Cold War and the Bomb
Thirteen days when the world nearly ended

In October 1962, the US found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 150 km from Florida. For 13 days the two superpowers stared at each other. That was the Cold War: no direct war between the US and USSR, but constant fear, spies, proxy wars and enough bombs to wreck the planet.
How it started
The wartime allies split over Eastern Europe. The US offered the Truman Doctrine (1947) and Marshall Plan to resist communism. The USSR built a bloc of satellite states.
Two camps
The superpowers never fought directly. They fought through others: Korea (1950-53), Vietnam, Afghanistan. The doctrine of Mutual Assured Destruction held that a nuclear attack would destroy both.
Saved by individuals

During the Cuban crisis a Soviet submarine officer, Vasili Arkhipov , reportedly refused to agree to fire a nuclear torpedo. In 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov judged a missile alarm to be false and did not report it as an attack. Historians agree these were real near-misses, though details are debated.
Ending the crisis

Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed that the USSR would remove missiles from Cuba and the US would pledge not to invade. A secret part of the deal: the US would withdraw missiles from Turkey later. A hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up in 1963.
Did the US simply win by staring down the Soviets?

Myth: Kennedy forced a Soviet retreat with no concessions. Fact: the secret Turkey deal was kept hidden for years. Both sides compromised. Also, 'Cold' is misleading: millions died in proxy wars in Korea, Vietnam, Angola and elsewhere.
Meanwhile in India…
Neither camp
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The Cold War began after 1945. NATO (1949) faced the Warsaw Pact (1955). Wars were fought by proxy. Cuba 1962 was the closest call. India led non-alignment. Think about it Is nuclear deterrence a peace or a gamble? Was non-alignment neutral or just independent?
Decolonisation: Empires End
In 1945 empires ruled a third of humanity. By 1975 they were gone

When the UN was founded in 1945, it had 51 members. Today it has 193. Almost all the extra countries are former colonies. In about thirty years, one of the biggest political changes in human history took place.
The great shift
World War II had drained Britain and France. The US and USSR both pushed against old empires. Colonised people had also fought in the war and wanted freedom.
Different roads

India's freedom came via mass non-violent movements and then talks. Vietnam beat France at Dien Bien Phu (1954) after a long war. In Algeria, a brutal war (1954-62) ended French rule. Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah won independence in 1957 through strikes and elections. Britain used force against the Mau Mau in Kenya, with serious abuses.
Suez, 1956

Britain and France, with Israel, attacked Egypt to retake the Suez Canal. The US and USSR forced them to withdraw. It showed the old powers were no longer in charge. In 1960 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 1514, declaring colonialism must end.
Unfinished business

New states inherited borders that cut across peoples. Many faced coups, civil wars and poverty. Portugal held its colonies until 1974-75. Some historians call the continuing economic influence of ex-rulers 'neocolonialism' (a term of Nkrumah's, 1965).
Was decolonisation always peaceful?

Myth: empires handed power over politely. Fact: there were many wars: Algeria, Vietnam, Kenya, Angola, Indonesia. Even India's independence came with Partition, in which perhaps one to two million died (estimates vary) and about 15 million were displaced.
Meanwhile in India…
A tryst with destiny
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The UN grew from 51 to far more members. Roads to freedom differed. Suez (1956) showed old powers' decline. Many new states faced hard borders. India helped lead the Afro-Asian cause. Think about it Why did colonial powers lose will? Do old borders cause today's conflicts?
Mao's China
The man who unified China, then lost track of how many he lost

On 1 October 1949, standing on Tiananmen, Mao Zedong announced the People's Republic of China. 'China has stood up,' he said, according to the common account. He would rule for 27 years. The results were mixed and often terrible.
Victory
The Communists won the civil war against the Nationalists (Kuomintang), who fled to Taiwan. Land reform took land from landlords, and many were killed. China fought the US in Korea.
The Great Leap Forward

In 1958 Mao tried to leap into industry with village steel furnaces and giant communes. Bad planning, false harvest reports and forced grain collection caused a famine. Estimates of deaths run from about 15 to 45 million, commonly about 30 million. The exact number is debated. Mao stepped back, but kept power.
Cultural Revolution

In 1966 Mao urged young Red Guards to attack 'bourgeois' elements. Teachers, officials and intellectuals were beaten and humiliated. Schools closed. The Little Red Book of his quotes was waved by millions. The army had to restore order, and the chaos ended with Mao's death on 9 September 1976.
Afterwards

Deng Xiaoping took over and launched reform and opening in 1978. The Communist Party itself, in 1981, judged Mao as 70 percent right and 30 percent wrong, though that figure is a Party formula. Mao's portrait still hangs on Tiananmen.
Great leader or great disaster?

Supporters credit Mao with ending foreign domination, raising literacy and life expectancy. Critics (such as Frank Dikötter) stress the famine and terror. Both can be true. Estimates of famine deaths vary with the method. A myth check: the 'Four Pests' campaign, including killing sparrows, did upset the ecosystem and probably worsened crop losses, but it was not the main cause of famine.
Meanwhile in India…
Hindi-Chini and a border war
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember The PRC was founded on 1 October 1949. The Great Leap Forward (1958-62) caused famine. The Cultural Revolution lasted 1966-76. Deng began reform in 1978. The 1962 war shaped India-China ties. Think about it Can a leader's aims justify huge costs? How did the 1962 war change India?
The Space Race
A beeping ball the size of a beach ball scared America

On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 , a 58-cm metal sphere. It beeped as it circled Earth. People with radios could hear it. Americans feared Soviet rockets could now carry bombs. The race to space had begun.
Soviet firsts
The Soviets sent the dog Laika (November 1957) and then Yuri Gagarin , who orbited Earth for 108 minutes on 12 April 1961.
Kennedy's bet

Weeks later, President Kennedy told Congress the US would land a man on the Moon before the decade ended. In 1962 he said 'we choose to go to the Moon'. Apollo cost the equivalent of well over a hundred billion modern dollars. In 1967 three astronauts died in the Apollo 1 fire.
20 July 1969

Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed Apollo 11's lander on the Moon, while Michael Collins orbited above. Armstrong stepped out first. About 600 million people watched on TV. Six Apollo missions landed 12 men by 1972. The Soviet Moon rocket, the N1, exploded repeatedly and never worked.
From rivals to partners
In 1975, an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz docked in orbit. Later, the two nations built the International Space Station (from 1998). Today, private firms and many countries also launch rockets.
Was the Moon landing faked? Did NASA spend millions on a pen?

Myth 1: it was faked. Fact: evidence includes 382 kg of Moon rock, reflectors left on the surface that scientists still use, and independent tracking by other countries. Myth 2: NASA built a space pen while the Soviets used a pencil. In fact, pencils were used by both, and the Fisher pen was developed privately.
Meanwhile in India…
From a bicycle to Mars
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Sputnik (1957) started the race. Gagarin was first in space (1961). Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969. The rivals later cooperated. India went from a bicycle to Mars. Think about it Was the race worth it? What can India's low-cost model teach?
1989: The Wall Falls
A press conference mistake ended a divided Europe

On the evening of 9 November 1989, East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules. Asked when they took effect, he shuffled his notes and said, 'immediately, without delay'. He had not been told it was meant for the next day. Crowds rushed to the Berlin Wall. Guards, overwhelmed, opened the gates.
The cracks appear
In Poland, the union Solidarity won the June 1989 elections. In summer Hungary opened its border with Austria, and thousands of East Germans left through it.
Gorbachev lets go

Mikhail Gorbachev , Soviet leader from 1985, began glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). Crucially, he refused to use Soviet tanks to prop up Eastern European regimes, unlike in 1956 and 1968. So one by one, the regimes fell, mostly peacefully: the 'Velvet Revolution' in Czechoslovakia, and bloody in Romania, where Ceausescu was shot on 25 December.
Not everywhere
In China, the 1989 Tiananmen protests were crushed on 4 June. Beijing's leaders chose force and kept power. It shows the outcome was not inevitable. Germany reunified on 3 October 1990.
The Soviet end

Weakened by economics and nationalism, the USSR itself broke up. In August 1991 hardliners attempted a coup and failed. Boris Yeltsin rose. On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned and the USSR dissolved into 15 states.
Who ended the Cold War?

Some credit Reagan's pressure and his 1987 call 'Mr Gorbachev, tear down this wall'. Others credit Gorbachev's choices, the weak Soviet economy, or ordinary people in the streets. Most historians say many causes combined. Myth check: the Wall did not fall in one night by hand; much of it was pulled down over the following months and years.
Meanwhile in India…
1991: India's own turning point
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Eastern Europe's regimes fell in 1989. Gorbachev refused to use force. The Wall opened on 9 November 1989. Germany reunified in 1990; the USSR ended in 1991. India liberalised in 1991. Think about it Was it inevitable or lucky? Why did China differ?
Globalisation and the Internet Age
A steel box and a web page changed how the world trades and talks

In 1956 a trucker named Malcolm McLean loaded 58 metal containers onto a ship in New Jersey. It sounds dull. It made shipping so cheap that making a shirt in one country and selling it in another became normal. Then, in 1989-91, a scientist at CERN gave us the Web.
Boxes and borders
After the Cold War, trade barriers fell. The WTO started in 1995. China joined in December 2001 and became the 'world's factory'.
The Web

The Internet existed before the Web. Tim Berners-Lee , at CERN in Switzerland, proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 and it opened to the public in 1991. Google appeared in 1998 and Facebook in 2004. Smartphones, from 2007, put the Internet in billions of pockets.
Winners and losers

Globalisation lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, especially in Asia. But many factory workers in rich countries lost jobs, and inequality grew in many places. The 2008 financial crisis, then Brexit (2016) and trade wars, led many to ask if globalisation was going into reverse. Some call the new phase 'slowbalisation'.
Culture and data

Films, music, food and memes cross borders in seconds. Data became the new oil, and a few big firms hold a lot of it. Questions about privacy, misinformation and who controls the networks are now political issues.
Is globalisation brand new?

Myth: the world only got connected recently. Fact: the Silk Road, Indian Ocean trade and the Columbian Exchange were global. The 19th century saw a huge wave of trade too, which ended with World War I. What is new is the speed and the digital layer.
Meanwhile in India…
Reform, IT and UPI
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Containers made trade cheap (1956). The Web went public in 1991. The WTO began in 1995; China joined in 2001. Gains were uneven. India's IT and digital payments rose after 1991. Think about it What do we lose if supply chains shrink? Who should control data?
9/11 and the War on Terror
The morning the world's news changed

On 11 September 2001, nineteen hijackers took four planes. Two struck the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one hit the Pentagon, and one crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people died. It was the deadliest terror attack in history, and it launched two long wars.
Who did it?

The attack was carried out by al-Qaeda , led by Osama bin Laden , who had base camps in Afghanistan under the Taliban. Al-Qaeda had grown from the anti-Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s. It had already struck US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (1998).
Afghanistan, then Iraq
The US toppled the Taliban in weeks. In March 2003 it invaded Iraq, saying Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction. None were found.
A long war

The 'War on Terror' brought the Patriot Act, the Guantanamo prison and drone strikes. Bin Laden was found and killed by US forces at Abbottabad in Pakistan on 2 May 2011. In August 2021, after 20 years, US troops left Afghanistan and the Taliban retook Kabul on 15 August.
Costs and echoes

Hundreds of thousands died directly in the wars, with estimates varying by study. Millions were displaced. The Iraq war also helped create the space where ISIS grew. Terrorism continued in many countries, and debates about security and freedom reshaped airports and laws.
Did Saddam Hussein plan 9/11?

Myth: Iraq was behind the attacks. Fact: investigations (including the 9/11 Commission) found no operational link between Saddam's Iraq and the attacks. The WMD claim also proved false. Also: the Taliban's regime was separate from al-Qaeda, though it hosted it.
Meanwhile in India…
India had known terror already
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember 9/11 killed nearly 3,000. Al-Qaeda under bin Laden planned it. The US invaded Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003). The Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021. India had also faced major attacks. Think about it How should states balance security and liberty? Why is defining terrorism so hard?
The Rise of China
A fishing town became a megacity in one generation

In 1980, Shenzhen near Hong Kong was a small market town of a few tens of thousands. Today it holds over 17 million people and makes much of the world's electronics. Shenzhen is the symbol of China's economic rise.
Deng opens the door

After Mao, Deng Xiaoping let farmers sell surplus crops, opened special economic zones and welcomed foreign investment. He is credited with the phrase about not caring if a cat is black or white if it catches mice (a saying he used).
The world's factory

With cheap labour and big ports, China exported huge quantities. After joining the WTO in 2001, growth soared, averaging near 10 percent a year for decades. China became the world's second-largest economy in 2010. The World Bank says about 800 million people in China left extreme poverty since 1978.
A different model

China combined one-party rule with market growth. The 'one-child policy' (1980-2015) cut births but left an ageing population. China's population began to shrink in 2022. Under Xi Jinping (leader since 2012-13), China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), strengthened party control, and built a stronger navy.
Friction

Disputes arose over the South China Sea, Taiwan, trade and technology, and Hong Kong's 2020 National Security Law. The US sees China as its main rival. China argues it is reclaiming its place after the 'century of humiliation'. As of 2025, China remains the world's second-largest economy, but faces slowing growth and a property slump.
Is China's rise inevitable or fragile?

Some see unstoppable growth. Others point to debt, an ageing population and limited political freedom. Remember: China was the world's biggest economy for much of history before the 1800s, so many see this as a return. Caution: 'poverty reduction' numbers depend on the poverty line used.
Meanwhile in India…
Neighbours, rivals, partners
Five takeaways, two puzzles

Five things to remember Reform began in 1978. Shenzhen and the WTO powered exports. China became No. 2 in 2010. Xi's China launched Belt and Road in 2013. India-China ties remain tense but linked. Think about it Is rapid growth possible without political freedom? How should India deal with a powerful neighbour?
Climate, Pandemics and the Shape of the Future
Two things changed everyday life in a way no army did

In March 2020, much of the world locked down within weeks because of a virus. And the same decade is on track to be the hottest in recorded history. This last lesson is about the stories still being written.
The warming planet

Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide to the air. Earth has warmed by about 1.1-1.3 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s, according to major scientific bodies. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees, aiming for 1.5.
Effects

More heat waves, heavier rains, melting glaciers and rising seas. Poorer countries, which emitted least, often suffer most. Climate talks keep arguing over who should cut emissions and who should pay: this is the principle of 'common but differentiated responsibilities'.
COVID-19

The first cases were found in Wuhan in late 2019. The WHO declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Vaccines using new mRNA technology arrived in under a year. The WHO estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-21, far higher than the 7 million officially reported. Pandemics are not new: the 1918 flu killed tens of millions.
New powers, new dangers

Artificial intelligence advanced quickly after 2022. Debates continue about jobs, deepfakes and control. Meanwhile, wars, trade rivalries and shifting power shape the global order. Nobody knows how it ends. History does not predict, but it gives you better questions.
Do scientists disagree about climate change?

Myth: scientists are split. Fact: studies find overwhelming agreement among climate scientists that humans are warming the planet. The real arguments are about speed, local effects and the best policies. Similarly, 'pandemics are one-offs' is wrong: experts expect more, which is why surveillance matters.
